detail.title: Economic Complexity and International Trade: A Case Study on the State of Goiás (2010–2019)
detail.abstract: This paper aims to explore the relationship between economic complexity and the productive structure of Goiás, Brazil, particularly in the context of environmental issues within international trade agreements. To this end, the export agenda of Goiás was analysed using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index to assess the concentration of exports by partners and products. Through the collection of statistical data on the Goiás economy for the calculation of concentration indicators, it is revealed that Goiás' production structure is concentrated in primary products and mining and it has just a few trade partners, exacerbating its vulnerability to evolving environmental challenges and international regulations. This scenario demands a transition towards low-carbon practices and more sustainable technologies while preserving native vegetation and its ecosystem services. For large commodity producers like Goiás, this necessitates continuous diversification and sophistication of the productive structure to enhance economic complexity.

detail.abstract: The restoration of forest ecosystems is a pivotal strategy for addressing environmental challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and land degradation while fostering socioeconomic development. This paper examines the financial and governance frameworks necessary to scale up restoration investments, emphasizing their role in achieving sustainable land use. By integrating a Post-Keynesian perspective, it highlights the challenges posed by unvertainties, high discount rates, and illiquidity in forest investments. The study explores mechanisms like blended finance to mobilize resources and overcome market failures, presenting a comprehensive analysis of financial instruments and policies. The findings underscore the importance of aligning ecological, economic, and social objectives to ensure the viability and scalability of forest restoration initiatives, with policy coordination emerging as a critical enabler.

detail.abstract: We introduce elasticity into game theory. We focus on inelastic games, defined as those with inelastic best-response functions. By applying the contraction mapping theory under Thompson's metric, we show that inelastic games have almost ideal properties regarding equilibrium existence and uniqueness, global stability, adaptive dynamics, and comparative statics. This framework substantially advances the understanding of elasticity, fixed-point theory, strategic complementarities, and network games. We argue that elasticity is not merely a standard economic measure or a mathematical analogue to the derivative; rather, it serves as a powerful, unifying framework for analyzing strategic interactions and feedback systems.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a top-down stress testing framework for estimating the financial (stability) impact of nature degradation. The methodology links the three components of the NGFS conceptual framework on nature-related risks: nature, the economy, and the financial sector. In the first step, a shock on nature, e.g. water scarcity, is calibrated based on the macroeconomic impact of proxy scenarios of nature degradation. We then estimate the impact of this shock on nature on companies. For this, we modify the Merton model (Merton, Robert C. 1974) to account for the vulnerability of companies to nature. The resulting higher probabilities of default are the main driver of credit and market risk losses for banks and insurers respectively. While the framework we introduce is general and can be applied to multi-dimensional nature shocks and joint climate-nature shocks, in quantification we focus on water as a sub-category of nature. The results show that the financial‑stability implications of nature‑related disruptions can be quantified in a coherent manner. Losses are allocated according to sectoral, geographical and ecosystem‑service vulnerabilities. The framework delivers granular indicators – from sectoral production impacts to market revaluations and prudential ratios – supporting a wide set of analytical and supervisory applications.

title: Thermodynamic Crowding Out: Empirical Evidence of Energy Cannibalisation in US Capacity Markets (2024-2026)

detail.title: Thermodynamic Crowding Out: Empirical Evidence of Energy Cannibalisation in US Capacity Markets (2024-2026)
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and hyperscale data centre infrastructure is precipitating a novel form of resource scarcity in United States electricity markets. This paper analyses load forecast data from the PJM Interconnection (2024–2026) to test the hypothesis of "Thermodynamic Crowding Out" – the structural displacement of physical industrial capacity by virtual computational load within a physically constrained grid. We identify a statistically significant divergence: while the virtual load proxy in the Dominion zone is forecast to expand by over 100% by 2035, the relative share of the physical industrial base in the broader PJM region exhibits stagnation or decline. Crucially, this displacement is mediated by a structural discontinuity in capacity clearing prices, which spiked by approximately 800% (from ~$29 to ~$270/MW-day) in the 2025/2026 auction cycle, creating a prohibitive barrier to entry for low-margin physical industries. These findings suggest the US economy has entered a "Type 0.7 Trap", where financial claims on energy (capital investment in AI) exceed the physical system's capacity to deliver work (exergy). We conclude that without a Thermodynamic Additionality mandate, the capacity market will efficiently allocate energy to high-margin virtual assets (chatbots) at the expense of strategic physical capital (factories), creating a long-term drag on real GDP potential.

detail.abstract: The main purpose of this project is to carry out an exhaustive analysis of the economic and financial situation of Louis Vuitton Moët Hennessy (LVMH), one of the world's leading luxury conglomerates, based on its consolidated financial statements from 2011 to 2024. The study employs a dual approach: a strategic analysis of the luxury sector and an in-depth financial evaluation. The strategic component utilizes frameworks such as SWOT, PESTEL, and Porter's Five Forces to assess LVMH's competitive positioning and the external macroeconomic environment. The financial analysis focuses on operational efficiency, liquidity, and capital structure, utilizing vertical and horizontal techniques as well as fundamental ratios. Besides, a comparable multiples analysis is conducted by applying both the Classic method (weighted by net profits) and the Sell-side approach (weighted by market capitalization) within the French luxury sector. Furthermore, the research includes a crosscountry industry risk comparison by calculating relevered betas for a peer group of nine leading international luxury firms, isolating business risk to evaluate competitive capital structures. The findings highlight LVMH's operational resilience and provide a final investment recommendation based on the discrepancy between its intrinsic value and current market price. The findings highlight LVMH's operational resilience post-pandemic, its strategic use of leverage for major acquisitions-such as Tiffany & Co.-and provide a final investment recommendation relative to the current market price.

detail.abstract: The oil and gas sector has vastly impacted the global supply chain for generations. With this sector's contributions, there has also been an increase in the level of awareness of stakeholders globally concerning multinational's corporate social responsibility practices. In the wake of recent times, there is even more so a great deal of attention being placed on the environmental implications of the multinational corporations operating in the oil and gas sector. The perceptions of CSR to these MNCs are impactful, as the public at large can act to legitimize an entity's operations. These perceptions can influence the level of support, and financial returns of these entities. This comes at a time when the United Nation's 2030 Sustainability goals are closely approaching. Thus, this paper uniquely endeavors to explore not just the public at large's perspective, but it takes into consideration the different genders' perceptions. It enables those in the O&G field to implement policies more conducive to their diverse and often underrepresented stakeholders: women. It utilizes the Jamovi software to analyze O&G MNCs' environmental practices' perceptions globally. Data has been gathered from selected continents and regions using the non probability purposive quota sampling method. Through the Kruskal Wallis' method of analysis, findings reveal that female respondents were less satisfied with the CSR practices when compared to the male participants. This could be attributable to the fact that women tend to have higher expectations of CSR practices in addition to MNCs often carrying out performative ineffective forms of CSR such as greenwashing. This study allows its readers to have a more in depth understanding of how gender affects perception globally, allowing them to expand on the body of knowledge and also taking appropriate action to start addressing the lower levels of perceptions.

detail.abstract: Incident response (IR) faces increasing pressure to manage a high volume of threats with limited human resources. This paper proposes a transformer-based framework for automating key phases of the (IR) lifecycle by integrating Natural Language Processing (NLP) models into operational cybersecurity workflows. Rather than applying isolated AI techniques, the proposed approach formalizes how pre-trained transformer models can be systematically incorporated into Security Operations Center (SOC) processes for incident classification, threat intelligence extraction, and response orchestration. The framework leverages transformer architectures fine-tuned on security-relevant data and integrates them into end-to-end (IR) pipelines. We evaluate this approach through a case study on phishing incident management, demonstrating measurable improvements in detection accuracy and response time compared to traditional manual workflows. Results indicate that transformer-based systems can reduce analyst cognitive load while enhancing both the speed and consistency of threat mitigation. In addition to empirical evaluation, we examine system-level considerations, including model explainability, false positives, and ethical implications such as bias and data privacy. The findings suggest that transformer-based (NLP) models can function as operational components within adaptive cybersecurity systems, enabling scalable and intelligent automation. We conclude by outlining future directions for extending this framework with multimodal models and advanced AI integration, emphasizing the importance of maintaining human oversight in AI-driven security environments.

detail.abstract: File managers are essential utilities in modern operating systems that allow users to organize, navigate, and manipulate files and directories. However, most traditional file managers primarily focus on graphical user interfaces and lack integration with developer-oriented workflows commonly used in terminal environments. This paper presents the design and implementation of a Rust-based cross-platform file manager that integrates both Terminal User Interface (TUI) and Graphical User Interface (GUI) environments within a unified architecture. detail.title: Alberta and the Regional Transmission of Canadian Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: Federal monetary policy is set for Canada as a whole, but its transmission depends on provincial industrial structure, housing exposure, and household balance sheets. Monthly province-level local projections using public Statistics Canada and Bank of Canada data from 2001 onward are used to compare Alberta with the rest of Canada under three complementary designs: a province panel with an Alberta interaction, a panel with continuous exposure interactions, and an Alberta-minus-rest-of-Canada differential specification. The strongest result is a persistent Alberta relative price-level response that remains visible in the most transparent robustness check. Labour-market differentials are present but less stable, while housing-start estimates are imprecise. The evidence is most consistent with viewing Alberta as a high-exposure region within a common monetary system, with energy exposure, construction intensity, and household debt service jointly shaping heterogeneous transmission.

title:
Legibility Layers of u-Kama 
A Layered Framework for External Comprehension Without Internal Compromise

detail.title:
Legibility Layers of u-Kama 
A Layered Framework for External Comprehension Without Internal Compromise
detail.abstract:
u-Kama is an ecological-monetary coordination system in which ecological truth is recognised through time-bound, place-bound verification rather than inferred through prices, institutional authority, or consensus mechanisms. This introduces a fundamental design tension: the system must be legible to external participants, institutions, and capital, while simultaneously preventing those actors from influencing ecological verification, qualification, or state transitions. 
This paper introduces the Legibility Layers Framework, a formal architecture that partitions u-Kama into distinct domains of external intelligibility. Each layer defines what may be understood and engaged with by specific audiences, while preserving strict non-interference with the ecological core. Drawing on insights from Hayek's knowledge problem, Goodhart's law, and Ostrom's governance of commons, the framework demonstrates how legibility can be structured without collapsing into manipulability.

title: Finite-Sample Properties of the Campbell and Thompson Out-of-Sample R2
affiliations: Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP) and IESEG School of Management

detail.title: Finite-Sample Properties of the Campbell and Thompson Out-of-Sample R2
detail.abstract: We study finite-sample properties of the Campbell and Thompson (2008) out-of-sample R2 statistic (R2OOS). We derive analytical approximations for its expected value under rolling and expanding window estimation. R2OOS is downward biased relative to the true level of predictability, and negative values of R2OOS can arise frequently under weak predictability. Simulations confirm the accuracy of the approximations and describe the full distribution of R2OOS under different data generating processes. We discuss an empirical application to equity premium  predictors.

detail.title: Green Patenting Takes Time to Pay Off. A Quasi-Experimental Study on the Italian Machinery Industry

detail.abstract: Despite extensive research on the relationship between environmental innovation and firm performance, there is still uncertainty about whether and when adopting eco-friendly practices pays off. To address this gap, we investigate whether green patents confer an incremental growth premium relative to other innovations and whether this premium follows a distinct, and possibly more delayed, temporal profile. Using a panel of 6,148 Italian machinery and equipment manufacturers (NACE 28) observed from 2014 to 2023 and a flexible conditional Difference-inDifferences (DID) approach, we estimate the dynamic effects of patenting on firm sales performance. The results indicate that general patenting leads to positive and persistent gains, with effect sizes that become larger at longer horizons. Additionally, green patents provide an extra growth premium that emerges only from the third year after the first green patent and is especially pronounced between three and five years after patenting. By revealing these dynamics, the study reframes the debate from whether it pays to be green to when firms can expect to benefit from environmental innovation.

title: Quantifying Climate Damages When Regions Trade: A Structural Gravity Approach
affiliations: , Institut Polytechnique de Paris, Georgetown University and Paris School of Economics (PSE)

detail.title: Quantifying Climate Damages When Regions Trade: A Structural Gravity Approach
detail.abstract: This paper presents a method for estimating treatment effects of local climate shocks when regions trade with each other. Because trade creates spillovers, comparing the change in outcomes of regions with different exposure to shocks leads to biased estimates. We model these between-region spillovers using standard assumptions from international trade theory, and develop a model-consistent strategy for estimating key parameters and deriving counterfactuals. We use our estimation strategy to revisit the literature on the impact of climate change on gross output. We find that accounting for trade spillovers yields substantially larger climate damage projections.

title: Trade Shocks and Media Slant

detail.title: Trade Shocks and Media Slant
detail.abstract: Does trade liberalization reshape the political language of local news? I scale over 52 million newspaper articles against the evolving political vocabulary of the U.S. House of Representatives and use an event study exploiting variation in NAFTA exposure across commuting zones. Trade-exposed newspapers underwent a systematic rightward shift: the share of Republican-leaning articles increased by 9.6 percentage points for a topversus-bottom-quartile difference in trade vulnerability. The shift is broad-not driven by trade-specific language-and appears across nearly all article categories. It emerges after NAFTA, persists through the sample period, and concentrates in low-education communities. Initially Democratic-leaning newspapers account for the entire shift, consistent with a demand-side channel in which newspapers adjusted to the changing preferences of readers in trade-affected areas.

title: Stewardship Governance Under Permanent Crisis: A Multi-Level Framework for Authority, Legitimacy, and Learning

detail.title: Stewardship Governance Under Permanent Crisis: A Multi-Level Framework for Authority, Legitimacy, and Learning

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a conceptual and theoretical analysis and did not involve human participants, human subjects research, or the use of confidential data. Institutional ethics approval was therefore not required.

detail.abstract: Contemporary governance increasingly unfolds under conditions of permanent crisis rather than episodic disruption. Yet dominant paradigms-centered on leadership, participation, technocratic optimization, or emergency authority-continue to assume that crises are bounded, legitimacy can be readily replenished, and institutions can reset once disruption subsides. This article advances stewardship governance as a multi-level framework for exercising authority, conserving legitimacy, and institutionalizing learning under conditions of persistent stress. Under permanent crisis, authority normalizes, legitimacy is cumulatively depleted, and escalation often substitutes for reflection. Stewardship governance reframes authority as custodial rather than consumptive, legitimacy as finite rather than endlessly renewable, and learning as a governing obligation rather than a corrective after failure. Integrating four complementary perspectives-Public Service, Constitutional, Civic, and Multi-Polar Stewardship-the article develops a multi-level framework tracing how governance failures and capacities propagate across administrative, constitutional, civic, and international domains. The article contributes to governance theory by identifying normalization, legitimacy depletion, and learning failure as systemic risks under persistent crisis and by demonstrating how stewardship can be operationalized through decision discipline, authority gating, dissent protection, and structured review mechanisms. Rather than promising crisis resolution, stewardship governance emphasizes preserving institutional capacity and democratic viability over time.

title: When Technology Meets Humanity: Shifting Policy Towards Protection in Conflict
affiliations: Emory University School of Law and Interdisciplinary Center (IDC Herzliya) - Lauder School of Government, Diplomacy and Strategy

detail.title: When Technology Meets Humanity: Shifting Policy Towards Protection in Conflict
detail.abstract:
New and emerging technologies offer significant contributions toward facilitating the end of conflict and protecting and easing the effects of conflict on the civilian population.  Over the past decade and more, security and legal scholars have devoted enormous attention to the role of new technologies in targeting and surveillance, including GPS-guided weapons, battle networks, collateral damage estimation methodology (CDEM), cyber, drones, and autonomous weapons.  In contrast to this focus on the use and effects of such capabilities in the conduct of hostilities, however, the potential for emerging technologies to enhance humanitarian and security objectives at the end of conflict—just as they already do effectively in disaster management and relief —has received little to no attention.

For several years, our End of War Project explored and highlighted the role that new and emerging technologies can play as protective and cooperative tools as conflicts end or begin to end. Based on academic research and multi-stakeholder consultations with legal, security, and humanitarian experts, the End of War Project’s white paper, titled “When Technology Meets Humanity: Shifting Policy Towards Protection in Conflict,” advocates for harnessing new and emerging technologies to promote humanitarian values at the end of conflict. Drawing attention to a scholarly and policy gap related to the use of technology at the end of war, the white paper provides real-life illustrations (such as how technology has been used to limit human trafficking or enhance the protection of humanitarian actors) and recommendations to drive a policy shift and encourage the development and deployment of new technologies for protective purposes during and at the end of conflict.

title: Restricting Temporary Contracts Increases Firm-Provided Training: Evidence from Spain
affiliations: Indeed.com, IZA and

detail.title: Restricting Temporary Contracts Increases Firm-Provided Training: Evidence from Spain
detail.abstract: We examine whether restricting temporary contracts increases firms' investment in worker training, exploiting Spain's 2022 labour market reform. Using 3.1 million online job postings from 2018 to 2024, we implement a difference-in-differences design that leverages pre-reform variation in reliance on temporary contracts across occupations. More exposed occupations shifted toward permanent hiring and increased advertised training relative to less exposed occupations. Training rose by 4.3 percentage points, fully closing the pre-reform gap by 2024. These results provide evidence that longer expected employment duration increases firms' investment in training, identifying a channel through which labour market regulation can shape human capital formation.

title: Outperforming A Benchmark With Α-Bregman Wasserstein Divergence
affiliations: and Université Laval

detail.title: Outperforming A Benchmark With Α-Bregman Wasserstein Divergence
detail.abstract: We consider the problem of active portfolio management, where an investor seeks the portfolio with maximal expected utility of the difference between the terminal wealth of their strategy and a proportion of the benchmark's, subject to a budget and a deviation constraint from the benchmark portfolio. As the investor aims at outperforming the benchmark, they choose a divergence that asymmetrically penalises gains and losses as well as penalises underperforming the benchmark more than outperforming it. This is achieved by the recently introduced α-Bregman-Wasserstein divergence, subsuming the Bregman-Wasserstein and the popular Wasserstein divergence. We prove existence and uniqueness, characterise the optimal portfolio strategy, and give explicit conditions when the divergence constraints and the budget constraints are binding. We conclude with a numerical illustration of the optimal quantile function in a geometric Brownian motion market model.

title: Insider Trading and Outcome Manipulation and Event Integrity in Prediction Markets

detail.title: Insider Trading and Outcome Manipulation and Event Integrity in Prediction Markets
detail.abstract:
This paper argues that prediction markets should not be governed by vague, imprecise, or poorly fit rules, and that debates over so-called insider trading in these markets are too often framed at the wrong level of analysis. The central regulatory question is not what trading should be permitted by default. The default is permission. The real question is what kinds of conduct should be prohibited.

The paper proposes a fit-for-purpose framework built around two distinct forms of market harm. The first is prohibited informational asymmetry: which kinds of informational advantage the law should forbid traders from monetizing in prediction markets. The second is outcome manipulation and event integrity risk: how to reduce the threat that the underlying event will be corrupted, distorted, or otherwise compromised in a way that defeats the legitimacy of the contract itself. These are different problems, and they require different, tailored rules.

Using prediction markets, and especially sports contracts, as a case study, the paper shows why conventional insider-trading rhetoric is an incomplete and sometimes misleading way to think about market integrity in this context. It argues that sound regulation should distinguish between trading on information, on the one hand, and corrupting or compromising the underlying event, on the other. By separating these two categories of harm, the paper offers a cleaner framework for exchanges, regulators, and policymakers seeking to develop coherent rules for prediction markets.

title: The Digitization of Telecommunications Wireless Markets and its Impacts on Market Structure
affiliations: Orange and Orange

detail.title: The Digitization of Telecommunications Wireless Markets and its Impacts on Market Structure
detail.abstract: The digitization of telecommunications markets has profoundly changed the nature of competition. These changes have been so rapid that regulations haven't had time to fully adapt. Digitization has shifted wireless industry from voice driven to data driven ecosystem of services, which is disrupting many aspects. On the one hand, data demand is much more elastic than voice demand, which vanished and even reversed the correlation between prices and average revenue per user (ARPU). On the other hand, technical progress is significantly faster for data than for voice, which increases non price competition (quality or cost reducing competition). This requires substantial and sustained investments and generates high dynamic effects that favors more concentrated market structure. This needs to be more considered in sectoral regulation and in merger guide lines.

title: The Welfare Effects of Work Restrictions for Disability Benefit Claimants: Evidence from the UK
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Welfare Effects of Work Restrictions for Disability Benefit Claimants: Evidence from the UK
detail.abstract: This paper examines the welfare effects of work restrictions in disability benefit programs. Work restrictions can disincentivize people with high work capability from applying and therefore control fiscal costs. However, they can also distort the labor supply of claimants. I study the UK setting, which features two types of disability benefits: transfers that compensate for the extra costs of disability without work restrictions, and work-restricted income replacement benefits. I ask whether incorporating the non-workrestricted benefits is welfare-improving. I find that non-work restricted benefits are well-targeted in the sense that less than 1% of payments go to those in the top 20% of the household income distribution, and non-distortionary, in the sense that transitions onto benefits have small effects on beneficiaries' labor supply. I then quantify the welfare effects of policy changes which increase the generosity of non-work restricted benefits, either by raising taxes or by reducing the generosity or work-restricted benefits, using both a sufficient statistics approach and a lifecycle structural model. I find that across all policy experiments, increasing the generosity of non work-restricted disability benefits is welfare-improving.

title: Love, Attachment, and Anxiety: Mengelola Cinta Dan Kecemasan Dalam Bingkai Pendekatan Bimbingan Dan Konseling Menelusuri Dinamika Relasi Romantis Remaja
affiliations: Universitas Negeri Makassar

detail.title: Love, Attachment, and Anxiety: Mengelola Cinta Dan Kecemasan Dalam Bingkai Pendekatan Bimbingan Dan Konseling Menelusuri Dinamika Relasi Romantis Remaja

declarations.funderStatement: Diri sendiri

detail.abstract: This study aims to examine the dynamics of adolescent romantic relationships through the interaction of love, attachment, and anxiety from a guidance and counseling perspective. The research employs a qualitative approach using a literature review method based on relevant scientific sources from the last decade. The findings indicate that adolescent romantic relationships represent a complex emotional developmental process, in which attachment patterns particularly attachment anxiety play a dominant role in determining relationship quality and adolescents' mental health. Attachment anxiety tends to trigger insecurity, emotional dependency, and difficulties in emotional regulation. However, romantic relationships also hold significant potential as a medium for emotional learning and psychosocial development. From a guidance and counseling perspective, comprehensive and integrative approaches are needed to help adolescents develop selfawareness, manage anxiety, and build healthy relationships. This study highlights the essential role of guidance and counseling services in supporting adolescents to navigate romantic relationship dynamics in an adaptive manner.

title: Cohort Welfare Accounting in Policy Transitions

detail.title: Cohort Welfare Accounting in Policy Transitions

detail.abstract: This paper develops a tractable welfare accounting framework for policy transitions in overlapping generations economies. I study policy changes that move the economy between steady states and generate transition paths with heterogeneous effects across cohorts. The framework expresses cohort-specific consumption equivalent welfare changes as an exact decomposition into a financial wealth component, a human wealth component, and an annuity factor component. This decomposition turns transition welfare comparisons into economically interpretable objects. I apply the framework to fiscal consolidations under alternative debt targets, debt maturities, and fiscal closures. Long-maturity debt amplifies announcement-time asset revaluation and materially changes the cross-cohort incidence of consolidation. With nominal debt, inflation-induced valuation effects further reshape cohort welfare, and their incidence depends sharply on whether adjustment takes place through taxes or spending. I also show how a lump-sum redistribution benchmark can separate efficiency from redistribution along the transition. The paper contributes a transparent benchmark for cohort-level welfare analysis in dynamic policy transitions.

title: Analyst Visibility and Earnings Forecast Quality
affiliations: Singapore Management University - School of Accountancy, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, New York University (NYU) - New York University (NYU), Shanghai and Singapore Management University - School of Accountancy

detail.title: Analyst Visibility and Earnings Forecast Quality

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming at Review of Accounting Studies

detail.abstract: This study examines how a reduction in analysts' visibility, resulting from brokerage houses' switch to anonymous forecasts on Eikon, affects earnings forecast quality. Using a differencein-differences design, we find that treatment analysts respond by issuing more accurate forecasts in the post-anonymization period. Treatment analysts who improve forecast quality the most are able to sustain visibility, as reflected in their coverage by the financial media, enhance their likelihood of being voted as star analysts, and induce greater client trading activities. These results are consistent with analysts' incentives to offset the reduced visibility so as to advance their professional careers and increase trading commissions for their brokerage houses. We further show that treatment analysts use a set of visibility-enhancing strategies including issuing broader and more frequent forecasts and setting bolder target prices. Our findings suggest that reduced visibility can prompt analysts to respond strategically in ways that can improve information quality.

title: Random Factor Ensembles for Robust High-Dimensional Macroeconomic Forecasting
affiliations: University of New South Wales (UNSW) and University of Sydney

detail.title: Random Factor Ensembles for Robust High-Dimensional Macroeconomic Forecasting
detail.abstract: This paper proposes Random Factor Ensembles (RFE) for forecasting macroeconomic aggregates from high-dimensional predictor panels. Unlike global principal component (PC) regression, which suffers collinearity distortions under redundancy and weak cross-loadings (Ng & Boivin 2006), RFE applies principal component analysis locally within randomly drawn predictor subsets before averaging across ensemble members. This structured projection reduces the noise propagation inherent in raw random-subspace (RS) regression (Boot & Nibbering 2019) while preserving subspace diversity. Under factor-rich data-generating processes we establish that RFE attains strictly lower asymptotic mean squared forecast error (MSFE) than both global PC and RS methods. Monte Carlo evidence confirms robust bias-variance improvements across sparse and dense specifications. Applied to U.S. industrial production growth using 130 monthly FRED-MD predictors, RFE delivers statistically significant forecast error reductions relative to PC and RS benchmarks, implicitly up-weighting real-activity predictors at short horizons and inflation and credit-spread series at longer horizons without researcher pre-specification.

title: Screening with Cash Deposits in Digital Credit Markets
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley, Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Screening with Cash Deposits in Digital Credit Markets
detail.abstract: We study a loan contract that requires borrowers to make a temporary cash deposit prior to disbursement, which is fully refunded and does not alter repayment incentives. In a randomized controlled trial with a digital lender, applicants are offered otherwise identical loans with or without a deposit. The deposit requirement reduces loan take-up but substantially improves repayment and lender profitability. The results indicate that deposits screen borrowers on both observable and unobservable characteristics. Higher-risk borrowers are less likely to take up deposit loans, and among borrowers with the same observable risk profile, those who accept deposit loans repay at higher rates, with the largest differences among low-risk borrowers. These findings show that simple contract features can complement data-driven credit models by adding an additional screening margin.

title: The Financial Burden of Regulation: Impact of Regulatory Intensity on the Cost of Equity
affiliations: , University of South Carolina - Moore School of Business, Bryant University and Bryant University

detail.title: The Financial Burden of Regulation: Impact of Regulatory Intensity on the Cost of Equity
detail.abstract: Using a comprehensive firm-level measure of regulatory intensity from Kalmenovitz (2023), we investigate how regulation affects firms' cost of equity for 2,803 firms from 2002 to 2019. We document that higher regulatory intensity raises the cost of equity, indicating that shareholders view regulations as a net cost. Results are robust to addressing endogeneity. We further explore the conditional effects of financial constraints, governance structures, corporate strategies, and political ties, highlighting the trade-offs between the benefits and costs of regulation. Overall, our findings provide new evidence on shareholders' reactions to regulatory intensity and offer important implications for policymakers designing regulatory frameworks.

title:
Voter-Authorized Debt and the Cost of Outstanding Municipal Bonds: 
Evidence from Texas School District Referenda
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University

detail.title:
Voter-Authorized Debt and the Cost of Outstanding Municipal Bonds: 
Evidence from Texas School District Referenda
detail.abstract: Does voter-authorized new debt affect the secondary market pricing of the issuer's outstanding bonds? Using 4,870 Texas school bond referenda matched to 4.3 million MSRB secondary market trades across 792 CUSIP-6 issuers, I exploit the discontinuous assignment of bond passage at the 50% majority threshold in a regression discontinuity design. In a panel specification with election and week fixed effects, referendum passage widens yield spreads on outstanding bonds by 12 basis points (t = 2.41). The effect materializes gradually over 12 weeks, consistent with the institutional timeline of post-authorization debt issuance. The effect is concentrated in building bonds (new construction, β = 0.18, p < 0.01) and absent for refunding bonds, consistent with debt dilution. Placebo threshold tests at 35%, 40%, 45%, 55%, 60%, and 65% are all insignificant.

title: Credit Expansion and Neighborhood Transformation: Evidence from Place-based Mortgage Lending
affiliations: University of Oxford - Said Business School and Pennsylvania State University

detail.title: Credit Expansion and Neighborhood Transformation: Evidence from Place-based Mortgage Lending
detail.abstract: When mortgage credit expands, who captures the gains? In supply-constrained markets, credit subsidies shift housing demand and are capitalized into house prices, enriching incumbent owners while leaving new buyers no better off. We document a fundamentally different mechanism when supply is elastic. Exploiting the Duty to Serve program, which expanded GSE mortgage purchases in underserved rural areas, we find that credit expansion increased homeownership and transaction volumes while property-level prices remained stable. This quantity response enabled neighborhood transformation through household sorting: low-skilled residents moved in while high-skilled residents remained. A spatial equilibrium model reveals that the policy reduces the effective cost of homeownership by 3.3\%. Elastic rural housing supply and low tenure switching costs pass these gains through to household welfare rather than prices. However, the effects are uneven: low-skilled owners benefit most, while high-skilled renters incur modest losses.

title: How Much of Earnings Information is Factor Compensation? How Much of Earnings Information is Factor Compensation?
affiliations: Rutgers Business School - Rutgers University

detail.title: How Much of Earnings Information is Factor Compensation? How Much of Earnings Information is Factor Compensation?
detail.abstract: Earnings surprises generate well-documented abnormal returns, but what fraction of this apparent information content reflects genuine news versus compensation for systematic risk factors? We address this question through a comprehensive decomposition using five abnormal return models—from Ball and Brown's (1968) simple market adjustment through the Fama-French-Carhart four-factor specification—applied to 2,358 U.S. firms with December 2023 fiscal year-ends. Testing 20 specifications that combine five models, two surprise measures (analyst-based and time-series), and two event definitions, we document a striking attenuation pattern: under time-series surprises, the good-news/bad-news spread declines from 12.98 percentage points to 0.16 percentage points as the model moves from simple market adjustment to four-factor adjustment—a reduction of 99%. Even analyst-based surprises attenuate by 65%, from 9.00 to 3.15 percentage points. Analyst-based surprises survive four-factor adjustment; time-series surprises do not. Post-earnings announcement drift approximately doubles the spread by month +12 and concentrates overwhelmingly in small-capitalization stocks (14.25 percentage points of drift versus 3.03 for large caps), consistent with limited-attention theories. Cross-sectional regressions confirm the predictive power of analyst surprises after controlling for size, book-to-market, momentum, analyst coverage, earnings volatility, leverage, and industry fixed effects. These findings carry direct implications for portfolio construction around earnings events.

title: Market Depth and Execution Delays
affiliations: , Wilfrid Laurier University - Lazaridis School of Business and Economics and Paris Dauphine University

detail.title: Market Depth and Execution Delays
detail.abstract: A trader using a limit order instead of a market order saves the bid–ask spread but faces execution delay while adding to market depth. We develop a dynamic order book equilibrium model to study the relation between market depth and execution delay. Greater limit-order usage increases depth but lengthens queues before execution. Using NYSE limit order book data, we confirm a positive relation between depth and delay. Their joint increase blurs market quality assessment, which is typically associated with high depth and low execution delays. Model-based welfare analysis shows that when depth and delays rise, limit-order usage is inefficient.

title:
DEMOCRACY 2076: 
A Futurist's Design for Self-Governance in the Age of AGI, Cognitive Warfare, and Conscious Capitalism

detail.title:
DEMOCRACY 2076: 
A Futurist's Design for Self-Governance in the Age of AGI, Cognitive Warfare, and Conscious Capitalism

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. No part of this work was commissioned, funded, or influenced by any government, political organisation, technology company, or commercial entity. The views expressed are solely the author's in an independent research and futurist capacity.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper involves no primary human subjects research and requires no ethics committee approval. All sources are publicly available secondary materials, fully cited herein.

detail.abstract:
Democracy is the longest-running political experiment in human history — and the most constantly endangered. Born in the city-states of ancient Greece, refined through centuries of Enlightenment thought, tested in revolution and war, and extended — unevenly, incompletely, but directionally — to most of the world's population, it rests on a deceptively simple conviction: that the people who must live with the consequences of political decisions should have meaningful agency in making them. That conviction has survived every previous challenge that history has placed before it. The question this paper asks is whether it will survive the ones that the next fifty years will bring.

Those challenges are without precedent in democratic history. Artificial general intelligence (AGI) — systems that match or exceed human cognitive capability across all domains — is anticipated by leading AI researchers within a decade. Artificial superintelligence (ASI) — systems that radically exceed human intelligence — may follow within a generation. Cognitive warfare, as documented in this author's previous SSRN papers, is already restructuring the epistemic foundation of democratic participation. Digital identity systems are concentrating unprecedented power in state and corporate actors. Longevity science may extend human lifespans to 120, 150, or beyond — raising entirely uncharted questions about who votes, who governs, and whose temporal interests political systems represent. New forms of conflict — synthetic, cognitive, economic, and physical — are straining the international architectures that democratic cooperation depends on. And the ecological and resource crises unfolding in parallel may produce abundance or scarcity scenarios that stress-test democratic institutions beyond historical precedent.

This paper argues, from a position of grounded optimism, that democracy will survive — but only if it is deliberately reinvented, not merely defended. The democracy of 2076 cannot look like the democracy of 1976, for the same reason that the constitution of 1789 was not adequate to govern an industrial nation. The technological, social, and cognitive environment of governance has changed beyond the design specifications of eighteenth-century representative democracy. What is needed is not the abandonment of democracy's foundational values — popular sovereignty, individual rights, accountability, and the peaceful transfer of power — but the architectural reinvention of the institutions, mechanisms, and identity systems through which those values are expressed.

The paper introduces the Conscious Democratic Architecture (CDA) — an original framework for democratic redesign that draws on liquid democracy theory, digital identity infrastructure, cognitive sovereignty principles, AI governance architecture, and the philosophy of conscious capitalism. The CDA proposes five design principles for democracy's reinvention: Verified Presence (the resolution of the digital identity crisis), Liquid Sovereignty (the move from periodic representative elections to continuous, delegable, contextual participation), Cognitive Protection (the constitutional right to an unmanipulated epistemic environment), Temporal Justice (the extension of democratic representation to future generations), and Conscious Governance (the integration of purpose, ethics, and long-term thinking into the institutional architecture of political decision-making). The paper concludes with a vision of what democracy at 2076 might actually look like — and what India, uniquely positioned among the world's large democracies, has to contribute to its design.

title: Chasing Shadows: A Revisit of the Groundhog Day Stock Market Anomaly
affiliations: SEFE Energy GmbH, Kassel, Germany, University of Kassel and University of Kassel

detail.title: Chasing Shadows: A Revisit of the Groundhog Day Stock Market Anomaly

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors do not have any conflicts of interest to disclose.

Lukas Rode is pleased to acknowledge funding from Stiftung Mercator for a project entitled Forschungsverbund klimakompatibles Finanzwesen - Teilprojekt Kassel, grant number 20020201.

detail.abstract: We revisit the so-called Groundhog Day anomaly, which suggests that U.S. stock markets exhibit positive abnormal returns when an early spring is forecast on February 2nd. Using updated data from 1928 to 2021 and an improved methodological approach, including skewness-adjusted t-tests with bootstrapped inference, we find no evidence supporting this behavioural effect. While our results are robust to alternative specifications, an international comparison (NIKKEI, DAX and TSX) reveals no parallel effects, suggesting the anomaly is not driven by global sentiment. Contrary to earlier findings, we find that the Groundhog Day effect does not persist over time and lacks both statistical and economic relevance. These results contribute to the growing literature questioning the replicability of behavioural anomalies and highlight the importance of publishing robust null findings.

title: The Relationship between the Degree of State Regulation of Homeschooling and the Abuse of Homeschool Children (Students)
affiliations: National Home Education Research Institute

detail.title: The Relationship between the Degree of State Regulation of Homeschooling and the Abuse of Homeschool Children (Students)

declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethics approval was needed for this paper.

detail.abstract: Various scholars and policymakers have claimed that homeschooling must be regulated or controlled by the civil government to make sure that life goes well for homeschool students. Others have argued that political philosophy and empirical evidence show that private homeschool education should be left alone. This study examined whether there is a relationship between the degree of state control of homeschooling and the rate of abuse or neglect by the parents (or other legally responsible caregivers) of homeschooled children ages 6 through 17. The investigation considered the homeschool laws by state and whether they had a relationship to homeschool abuse. Regression analysis of 18 years of data from all the U.S. states found no relationship between the degree of state control or regulation of homeschooling and the frequency of abuse of homeschool students.

title: "Justice Reimagined, access to Justice Redefined beyond Courtroom, ADR a New Mechanism of Dispute Resolution in Modern Era" and Research Gate 2026
affiliations: Business School, The School of Science Management and Commerce

detail.title: "Justice Reimagined, access to Justice Redefined beyond Courtroom, ADR a New Mechanism of Dispute Resolution in Modern Era" and Research Gate 2026
detail.abstract: The traditional justice delivery system, characterized by procedural rigidity and delays, is increasingly being supplementedand in some cases transformed-by Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) mechanisms. This paper reimagines justice beyond the courtroom by analyzing ADR as a dynamic, participatory, and accessible model. It evaluates constitutional mandates, statutory frameworks, landmark judicial pronouncements, and emerging scholarly perspectives, including recent contributions by Dr. Archana Kanungo (2026). The study concludes that ADR represents not merely an alternative but a transformative paradigm redefining access to justice in the modern era.

title: Learning from International Trade: Asymmetric Cultural Transmission and Gender Discrimination
affiliations: and University of Alberta

detail.title: Learning from International Trade: Asymmetric Cultural Transmission and Gender Discrimination
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how trade partner affects the employment composition of firms. We document novel empirical patterns using Chinese Customs data linked to the industrial firms survey: Chinese firms trading with more gender-equal countries hire a higher fraction of female workers, but not when they trade with less gender-equal countries. The effect is more pronounced for new firms and for high-skilled female workers. We propose a model of learning that is consistent with the empirical findings, where firms have misspecified initial beliefs but can correct their beliefs over time by observing labour market signals. Upon encountering a foreign firm with more signals, a firm can expedite learning if it imitates its foreign trade partner.

title: Financial Interdependence and Currency Internationalization

detail.title: Financial Interdependence and Currency Internationalization
detail.abstract: Does China's financial opening necessarily involve currency internationalization? To study how incumbent (U.S.) and rising (China) powers compete under financial interdependence, we develop a model of reserve asset demand featuring network effects. Our analysis shows that asset liquidity and currency liquidity interact to shape the timing of RMB internationalization. At early stages of financial development, China benefits from issuing in dollar because participation in the dollar system enhances the liquidity of its asset. As China's financial markets deepen, incentives reverse: issuing in RMB allows China to internalize network effects and erode the dollar's dominance, leading to a discrete shift toward market fragmentation. The transition dynamics are further shaped by U.S. sanctions, financial repression, and the response of third countries. These results highlight how financial interdependence transforms cooperation into rivalry in the evolution of the international financial order.

title: Stable Polarisation despite Rational Communication: Recursive Social Learning with Diverse Priors
affiliations: University of Tokyo - Graduate School of Frontier Sciences

detail.title: Stable Polarisation despite Rational Communication: Recursive Social Learning with Diverse Priors
detail.abstract: The presumption that increased connectivity fosters consensus-often idealised as the 'wisdom of crowds'-sits uneasily with persistent social polarisation. Many explanations attribute this pattern to irrationality such as cognitive bias, motivated reasoning, or algorithmic amplification. We show instead that persistent disagreement can arise even under fully rational communication. In a computational multi-agent model of recursive Bayesian learning, agents treat others' opinions as endogenously generated signals and update beliefs accordingly. Without a common prior, social learning leads them to increasingly accurate predictions of others' opinions, yet disagreement persists. As others' opinions become predictable-a phenomenon we term 'vanishing surprise'-the magnitude of belief updating declines and the system stabilises in a state of persistent divergence. A systematic exploration of learning-rate asymmetries shows that this outcome is robust across a broad parameter region characterised by slow updating on out-group information and by a varying degree of contrarianism. The same mechanism parallels 'model collapse' in recursive machine-learning systems, suggesting that epistemic fragmentation is a general vulnerability of recursive learning systems lacking a shared external anchor.

title: The Allocation of Decision Authority in Three-stage Decision Processes with Applications to Artificial Intelligence in Organizations
affiliations: Waseda Business School and Senshu University - School of Economics

detail.title: The Allocation of Decision Authority in Three-stage Decision Processes with Applications to Artificial Intelligence in Organizations
detail.abstract: We study a three-stage decision process that consists of information acquisition, project choice, and execution of the selected project. A principal wants to choose and implement a proactive project, and hires an agent who chooses a costly effort at the information acquisition stage as well as a costly effort at the execution stage. What the principal can do at the beginning is the allocation of the formal decision authority over project choice, either to herself or the agent. We show that the principal may choose to delegate decision authority to the agent, however unlikely the interest of the agent is to be congruent with her interest, or however competent and experienced she is. We provide several testable predictions. (i) Delegation is more likely as the manager has discretion over both information acquisition and implementation. (ii) Delegation is less likely as opportunities for compromising improve. (iii) Whether or not the parties agree about the status quo matters: In particular, if their preferences about the default decisions differ, the organization is more likely to be decentralized for new project development as their interests are less likely to be congruent. We further discuss the extent to which our results on optimal delegation survive when artificial intelligence (AI) is deployed, distinguishing autonomous and nonautonomous AI. If AI can fully automate information acquisition or execution, delegation cannot be optimal, but it can be optimal if the agent remains responsible for execution. If AI instead supports execution by lowering its cost, delegation can survive.

title: Why do SMEs not Apply for Loans? Bank Loan Application behavior and Access to Finance in the Eurozone
affiliations: Zeppelin University, Národná banka Slovenska, National Bank of Slovakia and Zeppelin University

detail.title: Why do SMEs not Apply for Loans? Bank Loan Application behavior and Access to Finance in the Eurozone
detail.abstract: Non-application behavior for bank loans among European SMEs is economically more prevalent than loan application rejections by banks. Therefore, it should not be treated as a residual state but disentangled by its different reasons. Using microdata from the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (2014–2025), we document how firms choose and switch between loan application, discouragement, reliance on internal funds, and other non-application reasons. We combine an expected-utility framework with empirical estimations through multinomial and standard logit models. The main novelty is our ability to simultaneously investigate different types of non-application for bank loans, which are driven by differing forces. Discouragement manifests as a belief-driven channel of non-application, loan costs and the supply side drive another, cost-driven channel of non-application. By disentangling driving forces of non-application for bank loans as core element of the analysis, our study provides new evidence on why SMEs choose not to apply for bank loans. We highlight that these decisions can reflect diverse and contradictory underlying conditions. Our results are important for understanding and addressing these differing driving forces of SMEs bank loan application behavior.

title: The Dual-Track System for Cryptocurrencies in Mainland China and Hong Kong

detail.title: The Dual-Track System for Cryptocurrencies in Mainland China and Hong Kong

declarations.funderStatement: The author acknowledge the support of ANU Law School RA Pool Grant for research.

detail.abstract: China is likely the only major territory where a dual-track system has been adopted for regulating cryptocurrencies. In mainland China, cryptocurrencies have been completely banned since 2021 on both supply side and demand side, with one exception: a central bank digital currency, i.e. the e-CNY, issued by the People's Bank of China, the central bank in China. In the Hong Kong Special Administration Region, however, cryptocurrencies, together with certain other categories of virtual assets, have been treated with a more welcoming regulatory regime. While regulators emphasize the risks to investors and the overall financial systems associated with cryptocurrencies, hopes have also been attached in both places. For mainland China, the ban combined with the launch and expansion of the e-CNY enabled China to become a pioneer and key member in alternative currency and payment networks to those dominated by the US,. In Hong Kong, meanwhile, market innovation and development of virtual assets including decentralized cryptocurrencies have been nurtured to restore and establish Hong Kong's regional leadership in the global financial markets. These new balancing acts were taken to embrace opportunities but also invited certain challenges: some are embedded in other dual-track systems that we have seen in China's economic and social reforms in the past four decades, while the others are unique and new in an era of frequent and rapid flow of financial capital and human capital around the world.

title: Truthful Implementation in Interdependent Democracies
affiliations: , University of Cyprus and University of Cyprus

detail.title: Truthful Implementation in Interdependent Democracies
detail.abstract: Can a society reach truthful collective decisions when each citizen's preferred policy depends not only on their own type but also on the types of others? Despite classic impossibility results for general interdependent preferences, we show that on one-dimensional single-peaked policy problems truthful implementation is possible if and only if (i) citizens' values are majoritarian and (ii) the collective decision rule is aligned with those values. Majoritarianism requires a median-type notion of preference interdependence, while value alignment requires that the rule mirrors the evaluative standard citizens themselves use to form judgments about policy. Any departure-toward alternative (e.g. utilitarian or technocratic) principles, or toward majoritarian principles that are misaligned with voters' own evaluative standardcreates incentives to misreport and undermines truthful deliberation.

title: Are Green Bonds the New Quasi-Havens? Novel Evidence From Sentiment-Driven Volatility Spillovers
affiliations: American University of Beirut, affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: Are Green Bonds the New Quasi-Havens? Novel Evidence From Sentiment-Driven Volatility Spillovers
detail.abstract: We test whether green bonds behave as quasi-haven assets when crisis sentiment spikes, using COVID-19 as a natural experiment for health crisis, addressing a gap in the literature on sentiment-driven volatility spillovers. Using a Time-Varying Parameter Vector Autoregressive (TVP-VAR) model, we examine the connectedness between green bonds and major assets including the S&P 500, gold, and oil from 2019 to 2023. The findings indicate that green bonds became significant net receivers of volatility from the S&P 500, surpassing gold during the pandemic period. To assess the role of sentiment on market connectedness, we incorporate RavenPack's Panic and Media Hype indices in Granger causality tests, revealing both as significant volatility transmitters. Particularly, media hype shows strong causal influence on connectedness. A DCC-GARCH t-Copula model further shows that spikes in sentiment, especially in early 2020, coincided with changes in asset correlations. Although green bonds generally show low correlation with traditional assets, their co-movement with gold increased during periods of market stress, reflecting partial flight-to-quality behavior. This study contributes to the literature on green finance by demonstrating that green bonds not only fulfill ESG mandates but also exhibit defensive characteristics under systemic uncertainty and sentiment shocks.

title: Equitable Progress and the Regulation of AI
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University, Dickinson Law

detail.title: Equitable Progress and the Regulation of AI

keywords: Artificial Intelligence Regulation AI Governance Equitable Progress Algorithmic Fairness Inclusive Innovation Technology and Inequality AI and Social Justice Generative AI Policy Global AI Governance Responsible AI

detail.abstract: This chapter argues that equitable progress should underpin the regulation of artificial intelligence (AI), ensuring that technological advancements promote justice, inclusivity, and human dignity. Drawing on philosophical traditions, including Rawlsian justice, Habermasian discourse ethics, and Sen’s human capability approach, the chapter presents a normative framework for assessing the societal impact of AI. It explores tensions between innovation and equity, transparency and performance, accountability and liability, and economic gains and workforce displacement. The author surveys the regulatory models of the United States, the European Union, China, and Singapore, identifying barriers to global harmonization and opportunities for international cooperation. Special attention is given to generative AI, whose influence on creative labor and cultural production underscores the importance of preserving human agency and ensuring fair compensation. This chapter concludes that AI governance must be grounded in both moral and technical principles and outlines practical proposals for global governance, including transnational cooperation, capacity building, and participatory policymaking. Equity, the author contends, should not be incidental but central to how AI is developed, regulated, and deployed.

title:
Digital Platforms as Data Vendors
Evidence from a Large E-commerce Platform
affiliations: Rotman School of Management and Independent

detail.title:
Digital Platforms as Data Vendors
Evidence from a Large E-commerce Platform
detail.abstract: This paper studies a large e-commerce platform that has offered and commercialized seller-facing data analytics products. These products provide detailed information on customer sources and demographics as well as aggregate demand of a seller's product category. We find that sellers, especially small ones, are incredibly sensitive to the cost of data acquisition. This is despite its positive revenue impact and observed influence on positioning, marketing, and pricing decisions. Our analyses rely on high-frequency event studies as sellers adopted and used data analytics products, combined with quasi-experimental variation in the cost of data acquisition. A counterfactual simulation shows that a uniform reduction in the cost of data raises overall platform sales while reducing market concentration on the margin.

title: Did NEVI Close the Gap? EV Charging Equity 2018-2025
affiliations: University of Central Florida

detail.title: Did NEVI Close the Gap? EV Charging Equity 2018-2025
detail.abstract: The United States allocated $7.5 billion through the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure program with a Justice40 mandate that 40% of benefits reach disadvantaged communities. Those equity requirements were removed in August 2025. We mapped 86,285 EV stations to census tracts across five states and computed per-tract equity ratios from 2018 to 2025 disaggregated by charger type. The overall station equity gap improved from 0.41 in 2018 to 0.52 in 2021, then reversed and fell to 0.49 by 2025. During the NEVI period, the gap widened 5.2% for total stations. However, DC fast charging equity improved 13.8%, suggesting NEVI's highway corridor focus directed fast chargers toward underserved areas even as Level 2 deployment favored higher-income neighborhoods. Low-income tracts have roughly half the charging infrastructure per tract as non-low-income tracts across the entire study period.

title: Indigenous Preparation Practices, Consumption Frequency, and Consumer Perceptions of a Proposed Maize-Okara-Cassava Composite Flour for Tuo Zaafi Preparation in Northern Ghana
affiliations: University for Development Studies, University for Development Studies and Department of Food Science and Technology, University for Development Studies

detail.title: Indigenous Preparation Practices, Consumption Frequency, and Consumer Perceptions of a Proposed Maize-Okara-Cassava Composite Flour for Tuo Zaafi Preparation in Northern Ghana
detail.abstract: Tuo-Zaafi (T.Z.) is a thick cereal-based staple widely consumed in Northern Ghana. A cross-sectional survey of 361 experienced consumers (≥15 years of T.Z. consumption) was conducted using structured and open-ended questionnaires administered via Kobo Toolbox to examine maize flour processing practices, storage conditions, sensory perceptions, and acceptance of a maize–okara–cassava composite flour for T.Z. preparation. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests. Females constituted 83% of respondents. Maize soaking time before flour production differed significantly across regions (χ² (4, N = 361) = 177.02, p = 0.01) and tribes (χ² (15, N = 361) = 65.40, p = 0.01), with 42.1% soaking maize for 36 hours. Most respondents (73.4%) stored processed flour in sealed plastic containers at ambient conditions. However, 35.5% reported adverse textural changes during prolonged storage. To improve texture, 41% of respondents reported blending maize with cassava flour. Encouragingly, 52% expressed willingness to consume T.Z. prepared from maize–okara composite flour to enhance protein quality, whilst 54% were unaware of the superior nutritional value of bio-fortified yellow and orange maize compared to white maize. Additionally, 63% identified T.Z. as their primary household staple. The high frequency of T.Z. consumption and positive attitude towards maize–okara composite flour highlight a strategic opportunity for food system innovation. Incorporating legume-enriched composite flours into T.Z. production could increase dietary protein intake and support nutrition-sensitive interventions aimed at reducing malnutrition in cereal-dependent communities.

title: Corporate Tax Reforms and the Investment Channel of Monetary Policy
affiliations: University of New Hampshire and Bentley University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Corporate Tax Reforms and the Investment Channel of Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: Corporate tax cuts and interest rate reductions both stimulate investment, yet the interaction between these policies remains understudied. Using firm-level data, a novel tax treatment measure that captures taxable income dynamics, and narratively identified corporate tax policy shocks, we estimate that a one percentage point corporate tax cut reduces the investment response to monetary policy by approximately 11 percent. The effect is symmetric for monetary tightenings and expansions. A New Keynesian model with enforcement constraints accounts for this finding: higher taxes reduce after-tax internal funds, tightening borrowing constraints and amplifying investment responses to interest rate changes. The results suggest that central banks may require larger interest rate adjustments following corporate tax cuts.

title: Developing a gender-responsive livestock vaccine delivery systems in rural Ghana: what have we learnt for scaling?
affiliations: Gender at the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), affiliation not provided to SSRN, International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, CGIAR - International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Developing a gender-responsive livestock vaccine delivery systems in rural Ghana: what have we learnt for scaling?
detail.abstract: CONTEXTScaling remains a central objective—and persistent challenge—of development interventions due to complex dynamics that affect effectiveness at scale. Transforming inequitable social institutions, particularly gender norms, is increasingly recognized as critical for successful and equitable scaling, yet evidence on how to scale transformative approaches remains limited.OBJECTIVEThis article contributes evidence from scaling gender transformative and accommodative approaches in an animal vaccine project in Ghana. METHODSThe study adopted a mixed-method approach. We explored the impact on empowerment using the Women’s Empowerment in Livestock Index (WELI). We assessed changes in norms through qualitative fieldwork. The qualitative baseline involved 122 respondents (80 women; 42 men) and the endline 324 FGD respondents (188 women; 136 men). The quantitative baseline involved 600 respondents (100 men; 500 women) and the endline 792 (396 women; 396 men). RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS The findings suggest that: (1) targeting root gender norms can efficiently shift multiple inequitable norms; (2) transformative approaches outperform accommodative ones in enabling empowerment and equitable change at scale; (3) GTAs can become demand-driven by women and men when benefits are recognized; (4) scaling GTAs may help reach tipping points for sustained change across horizontal, vertical, and temporal dimensions; and (5) rapid transformative change is possible when community influencers are engaged, root norms are addressed, and benefits are demonstrated for all household members at scale.SIGNIFICANCEThis paper shows innovative evidence on how scaling gender transformative approaches can catalyse behaviour change for sustainable and equitable livestock interventions.

title: Closing the Income Gap Opens the Door to Robots
affiliations: Yildiz Technical University - Department of Economics and Yildiz Technical University

detail.title: Closing the Income Gap Opens the Door to Robots
detail.abstract: Does reducing income inequality encourage automation? Using data from 25 countries over 1993-2019, we examine how redistribution affects automation, measured by the robot stock-to-employment ratio. To address endogeneity, we use an instrumental variables strategy and find that increasing the income share of the bottom 50% accelerates automation, whereas redistributing away from the top 1% dampens it. Considering both margins jointly, redistribution-induced declines in the Gini coefficient increase automation on net. To interpret these findings, we develop a general equilibrium model featuring two opposing forces. Transfers to workers reduce labor supply, inducing firms to substitute toward robots. In contrast, taxing profits to finance redistribution discourages the supply of entrepreneurial skills, thereby restraining automation. When profit income is sufficiently concentrated, the labor-supply channel dominates, generating a positive net effect of redistribution on robot adoption, as is observed in the data.

title: The Tax Benefits of Pre-Tax Alpha
affiliations: AQR Capital Management, LLC, AQR Capital Management, LLC and AQR Capital Management, LLC

detail.title: The Tax Benefits of Pre-Tax Alpha
detail.abstract: We present new evidence that pre-tax alpha materially enhances the tax benefits of tax-aware long-short beta-one equity strategies. The positive effect of pre-tax alpha on tax benefits strengthens with leverage and investment horizon. Two mechanisms drive this result. First, pre-tax alpha accelerates the growth of net asset value (NAV), which leads to higher dollar tax benefits as the asset base over which these benefits are realized grows. Second, pre-tax alpha leads to creation of new positions, acting similarly to recurring capital contributions. Position creation also lowers the cost of transitioning a long-short strategy to a long-only portfolio. In combination, greater tax benefits, faster NAV growth, and reduced transition costs stemming from higher pre-tax alpha translate into significantly higher after-tax post-transition wealth created by tax-aware long-short strategies.
