title: PVCL: A semi-supervised 3D medical image segmentation method based on prototype-voxel contrastive learning
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: PVCL: A semi-supervised 3D medical image segmentation method based on prototype-voxel contrastive learning
detail.abstract: Semi-supervised learning has significantly promoted the development of medical image segmentation and alleviated the burden of obtaining costly expert annotations. In particular, contrastive learning-based methods have attracted considerable attention due to their excellent performance. Such methods not only explore semantic information in the local context of a single image, but also capture global semantic information across batchesor even the entire dataset. However, existing image-level and region-level contrastive learning methods fail to fully consider the treatment of fuzzy voxels near target boundaries during segmentation refinement. This limitation leads to insufficient exploitation of global information among samples and their contextual associations. To address these issues, we propose a target voxel screening scheme that selects the most representative feature representations across different segmentation samples by computing the similarity between voxel features and class prototypes. The selected voxels are then used for contrastive learning, enabling more effective capture of global contextual information. Based on this strategy, we construct a novel network termed Prototype-based Voxel Contrastive Learning (PVCL), which incorporates both class-level prototype contrastive learning and voxel-level prototype contrastive learning. Specifically, this framework leverages prototype-based metrics to select different regions predicted by the teacher–student model and uses them as positive and negative sample pairs for contrastive learning. Through the joint optimization of these two contrastive processes, feature discriminability and compactness are significantly enhanced, leading to improved segmentation performance. We evaluate the proposed PVCL on three widely used benchmark datasets and observe consistent improvements over existing baseline methods. In particular, experiments on the KiTS19 dataset demonstrate that PVCL achieves a Dice score of 93.55% with only a 10% annotation ratio. The source code is publicly available athttps://github.com/maybeQi/PVCL-voxel-contrastive.

title: Are Return seasonality Due to Risk or Mispricing? Evidence from Anomaly seasonality
affiliations: Hanken School of Economics - Department of Finance and Statistics

detail.title: Are Return seasonality Due to Risk or Mispricing? Evidence from Anomaly seasonality
detail.abstract: This paper reexamines return seasonality in anomaly portfolios. While prior studies interpret anomaly and industry seasonality as explaining seasonality in individual stock returns, I show that interpreting anomaly seasonality as seasonality of risk premiums is misleading. Instead, it is mechanically inherited from stock-level seasonality through characteristic-based portfolio construction. Using 125 anomaly long-short portfolios and 1,238 corresponding raw portfolios, I find significant seasonality at annual lags in anomaly returns. However, anomaly-based seasonality fails to price seasonality strategies in individual stocks, whereas a seasonality factor constructed from individual stocks fully spans seasonality in anomaly portfolios. This asymmetric spanning relationship implies that anomaly portfolio seasonality is a projection of seasonality of individual stocks.

title: A Multi-Scale Attention and Efficient ConvolutionFramework for Brain Tumor Classification in MedicalImaging Analytics
affiliations: OSTİM Technical University, OSTİM Technical University and OSTİM Technical University

detail.title: A Multi-Scale Attention and Efficient ConvolutionFramework for Brain Tumor Classification in MedicalImaging Analytics
detail.abstract: Accurate classification of brain tumors from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) isessential for clinical diagnosis and treatment planning, yet conventional convolutionalneural networks (CNNs) often struggle to balance feature representation, computatiothe Parallel Multi-Scale Network (PMS-Net), a deep learning architecture that integratesmultiple heterogeneous convolutional branches, including depthwise separable anddilated convolutions, with channel-wise attention mechanisms based onsqueeze-and-excitation (SE) blocks, enabling simultaneous extraction of local and globalfeatures while maintaining efficiency. The framework is implemented in TensorFlow, anopen-source machine learning library, and evaluated on a publicly available brain tumorMRI dataset, where images are classified into four categories: glioma, meningioma,pituitary tumor, and no tumor, using a structured experimental design to benchmarkperformance against conventional CNN approaches. Results demonstrate strongclassification performance alongside computational efficiency, indicating the model’scapability to capture complex tumor characteristics across varying morphologies.Overall, the study presents a robust and efficient deep learning framework for braintumor classification, highlighting the role of multi-scale feature extraction and attentionmechanisms in advancing healthcare analytics and supporting reliable clinicaldecision-making.

title: Transportation, Innovation and Growth
affiliations: University of South Carolina, Stanford University - Hoover Institution and Duke University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Transportation, Innovation and Growth
detail.abstract: This paper develops a tractable multi-industry model of endogenous growth with innovation in both manufacturing and transportation. When the per-unit cost of shipping goods is exogenous, the sales ampli…cation of manufacturing productivity improvements is weak and growth eventually ceases. When …rms allocate R&D resources to innovation in transportation, endogenous growth occurs because cost-reducing innovation in production and in transportation reinforce each other in a virtuous circle. Policies or frictions that raise per-unit transportation costs-such as cumulative regulation, infrastructure bottlenecks, or fuel price pressures-dampen the translation of productivity gains in the factory into aggregate growth. Conversely, lower per-unit transportation costs generate both level and growth e¤ects by strengthening the ability of …rms to turn process innovations into a larger volume of sales. More broadly, the results suggest that understanding growth requires treating production and distribution as an integrated system.

title: Financing the AI Buildout
affiliations: Columbia University Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Financing the AI Buildout

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no conflicts of interest to declare.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the AI boom is not only a software revolution but also a capital-intensive infrastructure cycle centered on data centers, power systems, cooling, and specialized chips. It shows that the scale of required investment is historically large and increasingly financed through a mix of hyperscalers, real estate developers, infrastructure funds, private credit, and structured finance. These arrangements expand funding capacity while shifting ownership and risk off balance sheet. The paper highlights how asset-level leverage, contractual complexity, technological obsolescence, and power and supply-chain bottlenecks may create new financial vulnerabilities as AI infrastructure becomes systemically important.

title: A Framework for Analysis of Credit Supply and Demand Shocks: The Case of Bosnia and Herzegovina
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Framework for Analysis of Credit Supply and Demand Shocks: The Case of Bosnia and Herzegovina

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human subjects or individual-level identifiable data and therefore does not require ethics approval.

keywords: A Framework for Identifying Credit Supply and Demand Shocks

detail.abstract: The paper uses a novel panel multi-level fixed effects empirical strategy to identify credit supply and demand shocks. The paper shows that banks with positive credit supply shocks on the margin expand their portfolio and engage in a risk-taking behaviour. The selected bank balance sheet variables have meaningful effects on the bank supply shocks. Moreover, the bank supply and demand shocks aggregated at the bank and industry levels have significant effects on the key macroeconomic variables. The author proposes a framework for the implementation of macro prudential and monetary policy based on the estimated credit shocks.

title: Closed-form Optimal Tontine Payouts in an Affine GARCH Model
affiliations: University of Western Ontario

detail.title: Closed-form Optimal Tontine Payouts in an Affine GARCH Model
detail.abstract: We consider a discrete-time tontine with proportional payouts, a bequest motive, and stochastic mortality, where a representative participant maximizes expected constant relative risk aversion (CRRA) utility of consumption and terminal wealth. To ensure a stable and operationally viable consumption path, we solve for the optimal pre-commitment payout rate (π t), leading to closed-form backward recursion based on the market portfolio's cumulative return moment generating function (m.g.f.). We show that the difference of such pre-commitment to the global optimal is economically negligible. An empirical illustration for a T = 35 year retirement horizon compares optimal payout profiles under an affine GARCH(1,1) model, a matched lognormal benchmark and an optimal risk-free cash account. The analysis demonstrates that ignoring dynamic volatility yields relative payout deviations of up to 4.5% at inception, with modest Wealth Equivalent Gain (WEG) from model mis-specification. The WEG could be up to 11% if acting optimal but avoiding risky investments. We also detect a WEG of up to 6.0% due to mismatch frequency, i.e., the operational rigidity of weekly rather than hourly administrative rebalancing. These findings, supported by robustness checks across major equity indices, underscore the necessity of integrating discrete-time GARCH dynamics with the proper rebalancing frequency into modern actuarial frameworks.

title:
When Politicians Stop Learning: 
Social Media and the Quality of Democratic Representation
affiliations: University of Turin - Collegio Carlo Alberto, University of Brescia - Department of Economics and Management and University of Brescia

detail.title:
When Politicians Stop Learning: 
Social Media and the Quality of Democratic Representation
detail.abstract: The political economy literature on social media has primarily focused on misinformation and polarization. We highlight a different and overlooked channel: the effect of data-driven voter profiling on politicians' incentives to acquire policyrelevant information. We develop a model in which an incumbent politician can exert costly effort to learn about an uncertain state of the world before proposing a policy to a representative voter. The politician does not perfectly observe the voter's prior beliefs, or opinion. Improvements in voter profiling, such as those enabled by social media, correspond to reductions in this uncertainty. The politician's learning effort increases her re-election chances through two channels: a quality effect, by improving the match between the policy and the true state; and a persuasion effect, by inducing voters to place lower weight on their opinion and thereby compressing ex-post disagreement across possible voter types. We show that the higher the politician's uncertainty over the voter's opinion, the stronger her incentives to exert effort to change it. Therefore, improved voter profiling lowers equilibrium learning effort and ultimately reduces the quality of democratic representation.

reference: Banque de France Working Paper No. 1024
title: Women-Led Firms' Access to Bank Credit
affiliations: Banque de France - Economic Study and Research Division and Banque de France

detail.title: Women-Led Firms' Access to Bank Credit

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banque de France Working Paper No. 1024
publicationDetails.journalName: Banque de France Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper documents the existence and evolution of a gender gap in bank financing among non-financial firms, disentangling demand-and supply-side effects. Using quarterly panel data for French firms from 2012 to 2023, we find that this gap is driven by the demand side: women-led firms are between 12% and 26% less likely to apply for bank credit, depending on the type of loan. However, conditional on applying, the probability of rejection for women-led firms does not differ significantly from that of men-led firms. Moreover, we find no evidence that the gender gap in credit demand is closing over time.

detail.abstract:
The study examines the phenomenon of ‘gamification’, defined as the application of game-like techniques in non-gaming contexts. The direct access of retail investors to financial markets via digital platforms and the widespread circulation of information on social media are posing new challenges for both regulators and supervisory authorities: gamification is significantly transforming investors’ behaviour, particularly that of retail investors, introducing major risks related to volatility and impulsive decision-making.

To fully grasp the implications of gamification in financial investments, key cases – such as GameStop and Robinhood – are analyzed, exploring their regulatory implications and existing regulatory gaps. Furthermore, pressing issues – such as the role of digital platforms, social media, and fin-influencers in shaping investors’ decisions – are discussed, along with an analysis of the inherent risks of copy trading and PFOF.

The surge in GameStop’s share price between May and June 2024 highlights the ongoing influence of social dynamics and underscores the importance of providing reliable information to ensure market efficiency and investor protection.

To enhance the protection of retail investors, this research papers proposes several updates to the regulatory framework.

title: Industry Perspectives on CO2 Transport Optimization Models and Case Studies
affiliations: , Delft University of Technology and RWTH Aachen University

detail.title: Industry Perspectives on CO2 Transport Optimization Models and Case Studies
detail.abstract:
Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is widely regarded as essential for decarbonisingprocess emissions in cement and lime production. It requires large-scale CO2 transport infrastructure. The design is often studied using mathematical optimization models. However, it remains unclear to what extent these models reflect the perspectives and constraints of the industry stakeholders.

This paper systematically contrasts a targeted review of CO2 transport optimization studies relevant for Germany with semi-structured interviews of German cement and lime producers. We derive common modeling components (transport modes, system boundaries, sinks, geographic areas, sectors, actor behavior) and use them to compare model assumptions and interview data.

We find convergence on pipelines as the dominant long-term transport option, offshore North Sea storage as a key ramp-up sink, a primary focus on permanent storage rather than utilization, and the strategic role of domestic onshore storage. However, industry experts additionally stress a rail-based initial phase, plant-specific business cases, the need for ‘sink resilience’, CO2 purity constraints, decentralized investment decisions, and social acceptance. These are dimensions that are mostly weakly represented in current models.

detail.abstract: United States labor policy is notable for how little it constrains most employers: unlike many jurisdictions represented in this volume, “atwill” employment is standard, and union density is low. In line with this general approach, federal lawmakers have not regulated AI or related technologies, either to plan for feared job displacements, or to limit the use of this technology to depress worker power through surveillance, discrimination, or other strategies. And while federal regulatory agencies previously took steps to bring existing law to bear in these new contexts, this approach is far from comprehensive. However, a handful of US state governments have shown greater willingness to regulate employers’ use of these emerging technologies – although their regulation occurs in the shadow of federal “preemption doctrine,” under which states are precluded from regulating some aspects of work law. This chapter explains why federal regulation of employers’ use of emerging technologies is unlikely and analyzes prospects for states to step into the breach.

title: Do People Have Economic Expectations?
affiliations: Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE, Frankfurt School of Finance & Management, University of Bonn and University of Cologne

detail.title: Do People Have Economic Expectations?
detail.abstract: Expectations are central to models of economic and financial decision-making. Yet in practice, individuals are often inattentive and, when asked, report fragile, context-dependent expectations that are only weakly linked to decisions. This raises the question to what extent they hold such expectations in the first place. Against this backdrop, we ask two questions: When people think about an economic issue, can they build on expectations they formed before? And does it matter if they cannot? We develop and validate a survey measure that distinguishes between individuals who can recall expectations formed in the past and those who must form expectations from scratch. We show that while many households have expectations about key economic variables, a large share of households do not - even among those close to decisions for which the expectation should be relevant. This matters: individuals without a previously-formed expectation (i) express expectations that are more context-dependent, (ii) update expectations more strongly but less persistently in response to new information, (iii) report expectations that are less relevant to decisions, and (iv) rely more on heuristics that do not require expectations when making economic decisions.

title: The Targeted Depletion Benchmark (TDB): A Constraint-Optimization Model for Labor Cessation

detail.abstract: Traditional personal finance literature predominantly focuses on capital preservation models, such as the Safe Withdrawal Rate, to mitigate longevity risk. While financially robust, these models often result in significant "over-saving," yielding high terminal wealth values that represent unconsumed labor utility. This paper introduces the Targeted Depletion Benchmark (TDB), a framework that synthesizes the Life-Cycle Hypothesis with "Coast" accumulation mechanics. We define a mathematical formula to identify the minimum critical capital threshold required to cease savings contributions early. By relying on compound growth to fund a risk-adjusted depletion strategy, the TDB model demonstrates that rational agents can achieve financial security significantly earlier than traditional heuristics suggest.

title: AI Financial Advice: Supply, Demand, and Life Cycle Implications
affiliations: , , Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: AI Financial Advice: Supply, Demand, and Life Cycle Implications
detail.abstract: We develop and implement a novel method to study personal financial advice from Large Language Models (LLMs). Studying this advice is challenging because it depends on the model used (i.e., supply), the questions individuals ask (i.e., demand), and their evolving circumstances. We address these challenges by surveying a representative sample of adults and asking them to write prompts seeking spending and investing advice from an LLM. We then simulate the lifetime paths that result from following this advice under realistic asset and labor market conditions. Applying our method to GPT-5.2 and Gemini 3 Flash, we document three facts about AI-generated financial advice. First, following LLM advice would move most survey respondents closer to the prescriptions of life cycle theory relative to their current behavior, including broader participation in diversified equity funds, equity shares that decline with age, and sizeable saving buffers. Second, replacing individual-written prompts with academic prompts moves LLM advice even closer to life cycle theory, with better consumption smoothing and less reliance on simple heuristics. Third, LLM advice varies systematically with individual characteristics, such as gender and financial literacy. These differences accumulate over the life cycle into wealth differences at retirement of 4-5% between groups and reflect both demand (i.e., systematic variation in the prompts written by different individuals) and supply (i.e., differences in advice for a given prompt). These facts highlight the potential of generative AI to improve financial decision-making, but suggest that its impact is likely heterogeneous across households and depends on how the technology is used.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of India's digital financial ecosystem-accelerated by the 2016 demonetization, the proliferation of UPI, and the mainstreaming of mobile banking-has reshaped patterns of financial participation across the country. Yet, young Indian women remain an understudied demographic whose adoption of digital finance is mediated by complex interactions of sociocultural norms, psychological constructs, and technological affordances. This paper synthesizes empirical evidence and conceptual insights from existing interdisciplinary literature to develop a human-centered analytical framework explaining digital finance adoption among women aged 18-25. The review identifies recurring determinants such as differential risk perception, trust asymmetries, digital and financial literacy gaps, gendered constraints on autonomy, and usability or interface-level frictions embedded in fintech platforms. By integrating these determinants, the paper advances a conceptual model that foregrounds emotional trust, cognitive load, perceived agency, and contextual social influences as critical mediators in the adoption process. The analysis contributes a consolidated theoretical understanding of gendered digital finance behavior in the Indian context and outlines design and policy implications for improving accessibility, inclusion, and sustained engagement among young women users.

title: A General Theory of Civilisational Governance Capacity Alignment and Progress as Governed Freedom under Finite Capacity

detail.title: A General Theory of Civilisational Governance Capacity Alignment and Progress as Governed Freedom under Finite Capacity
detail.abstract:
This paper advances a general theory of civilisational governability for systems that expand in autonomy, scale and energy under finite governance capacity. It defines F(t) as the expanding reachable action space enabled by computation, networked intelligence and energy. Governance intelligence I(t) is defined as the accumulative and decaying capacity to observe, verify and correct actions in time. Civilisational viability depends on the proportional relationship between these two variables. Alignment emerges therefore as a rate condition expressed through the governing freedom constraint which defines the proportional scaling required for civilisational viability. When freedom expands faster than governance intelligence accumulates, systems approach the governing freedom boundary, the geometric limit separating admissible from inadmissible trajectories. Beyond this boundary, corrective influence loses temporal effectiveness and structural horizon conditions emerge. Misalignment and irreversibility arise from geometric divergence between expanding action space and enforceable constraint. Because civilisational viability is rate-bounded by this constraint, real-time endogenous governance embedded within system architecture becomes a structural prerequisite. Distributed intelligence across Earth and orbit operates within unequal temporal frames in which action propagation can exceed corrective transmission, compressing the governing freedom boundary. Governability in space is therefore inseparable from that on Earth. Failure to maintain real-time proportional scaling guarantees structural horizon conditions irrespective of energy scale or expansion. 

Assets Under Governance (AUG) operationalises this constraint as a zero-trust operator that renders alignment observable and continuously measurable in real-time across artificial intelligence, institutions and sovereign systems on Earth and in orbital jurisdictions.

title: My Shop, My Agency: Self-Efficacy Enhancement and Women's Entrepreneurial Empowerment Through Social Commerce Platforms

detail.abstract: Entrepreneurship has long been theorised as a primary pathway to economic independence and social mobility. I have introduced the Self-Efficacy Enhancement Theory (SEET), an intervention-oriented theoretical framework that constructs an integrated account of platform-mediated women's entrepreneurial empowerment. SEET proposes that empowerment is best understood as a tripartite, dynamically interacting construct consisting of three co-evolving dimensions: psychological self-efficacy, the belief in one's ability to think, decide, persist, and regulate emotions under entrepreneurial pressure; social self-efficacy, confidence in one's capacity to initiate, maintain, and strategically leverage digital social relationships for commercial purposes; and economic self-efficacy, the belief in one's ability to generate income, interpret market data, and achieve financial independence through platform-mediated entrepreneurial activity. These three dimensions, according to SEET, co-evolve in a self-sustaining empowerment loop, in which progress in any one dimension creates enabling conditions for advancement in the other two.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the applicability of MARPOL Annex V to routine operational practices within the global leisure marine sector, with particular focus on the discharge of boat cleaning products in marina environments. While MARPOL Annex V is commonly associated with commercial shipping and garbage disposal, its provisions apply to all vessels, including non-commercial pleasure craft. Under Annex V, cleaning agents and additives may only be discharged into the sea if they are not harmful to the marine environment (Non-HME).

Through analysis of publicly available Safety Data Sheets, marina contractual documentation and insurance market commentary, this study identifies a structural compliance awareness gap within the leisure marine industry. A significant proportion of boat cleaning products marketed for routine use carry aquatic hazard classifications, yet the specific Non-HME discharge test under MARPOL Annex V is rarely referenced explicitly in marina operational guidance or berth-holder agreements. This disconnect creates potential regulatory and insurance exposure, particularly given that pollution coverage in leisure marine policies is typically limited to sudden and accidental events rather than routine operational discharge.

The paper does not suggest widespread deliberate non-compliance. Instead, it argues that a decades-old international legislative framework has not been clearly articulated in its practical application to everyday leisure boating activities. Proportionate awareness measures, contractual clarification and transparent product classification could materially reduce unintended legal and environmental risk.

Authored by Peter Wallbank, the research contributes to ongoing discourse on maritime environmental law, marina risk management and the development of boat cleaning products designed to meet Non-HME criteria, including emerging Oceans Assured™ compliant formulations.

title: The Anchor-Precision Effect in a Polarized World: Evidence from Field and Experimental Data
affiliations: , Academia Sinica - Institute of Political Science and National Taiwan University - Department of Political Science

detail.title: The Anchor-Precision Effect in a Polarized World: Evidence from Field and Experimental Data
detail.abstract: Public managers face a strategic paradox: how to minimize budget cuts from oversight bodies while maximizing public acceptance for inevitable price increases. We investigate the role of numerical precision as a solution to this dual challenge. Integrating 17 years of field data from Taiwan's government budgets (N = 18, 900) with two controlled experiments (N = 1, 350), we demonstrate that the optimal numerical strategy depends on the direction of adjustment. For budgetary defense, precision acts as a shield: precise proposals induce a fine-grained mental scale, resulting in significantly smaller legislative cuts. Conversely, for cost-imposing measures, rounding facilitates compliance: rounded anchors trigger coarser mental scales, leading the public to accept larger price adjustments. We provide causal evidence that the internal scale of adjustment mediates these effects. Furthermore, we identify government satisfaction as a key boundary condition: the anchor precision effect is significantly amplified among satisfied decision makers but attenuated among those with low satisfaction. These findings establish numerical framing as a potent choice architecture tool, allowing public administrators to strategically deploy precision or rounding to safeguard resources and manage fiscal compliance.

detail.abstract: We study how workers form inflation expectations and incorporate them into labor supply decisions using experimental evidence from the U.S. online labor market. Exploiting exogenous variation from randomized information provision, we find that higher price inflation expectations do not raise reservation wages. Instead, workers lower reservation wages for multiperiod contracts, even after controlling for wage growth and unemployment expectations. These patterns are consistent with a labor search model where higher inflation expectations reduce the perceived value of future job offers, increase income risk, and induce a precautionary reduction in reservation wages. Overall, the findings suggest limited risk of wage-price spirals.

title: Concentrated Wealth: The Inheritance License Market

detail.title: Concentrated Wealth: The Inheritance License Market

detail.abstract:
Thomas Piketty’s 2014 Capital gives academic rigor to the folk concern over the “1-percenters”, i.e., the owners of concentrated wealth.  Piketty argues that the personal ownership of wealth necessarily concentrates because the return on capital exceeds the rate of economic growth.  This matters because overly concentrated wealth threatens economies, politics and culture.  His solution is a modest annual tax on wealth, with the proceeds funding expanded state programs.  The aim of this paper is to propose a different solution that, minimally, serves as a thought experiment to better evaluate capitalism, kinship and constitutionalism.  

Every civilization must pass its wealth on to the next generation, employing a standard independent of desert for personally creating the wealth.  That standard is the right of families to monopolize bequest and inheritance.  The proposal is to break the family’s monopoly on inheritance but not on bequeathing.  All citizens should have a constitutionally equal opportunity to inherit the wealth created by persons no longer alive.  Institutionally, citizens would have to present a license to the state to inherit more than a particular threshold of wealth.  The inheritance licenses then trade on a market, with the net buyers being those who expect to inherit significant wealth and the net sellers everyone else.  The resulting price signals would change personal economic conduct in the right way, resulting in a ceiling and floor of the ownership of wealth, and one that sustains over generations.  An Inheritance License Market would prevent the pathologies of concentrated wealth better than either no corrective or Piketty’s wealth tax.

title: Monetary Policy and Taylor Reaction Functions: Business Cycles, Central Bank Governance and Central Bankers’ Preferences
affiliations: Bocconi University - Department of Economics, Bocconi University - Department of Economics (ECO)

detail.title: Monetary Policy and Taylor Reaction Functions: Business Cycles, Central Bank Governance and Central Bankers’ Preferences

publicationDetails.journalName: BAFFI Centre on Economics, Finance & Regulation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: A key tool has characterized monetary policy analysis over the past thirty years: the use of reaction functions. This paper aims to review the evolution of the economics of the monetary policy reaction function from Taylor’s (1993) seminal contribution to present day. The review is based on two assumptions: (1) the peculiar property of the Taylor rule as a flexible tool explains its pathbreaking nature given its capacity to test multiple economic and institutional cases; and (2) this property can be described using a theoretical four-pillar approach. In this approach, the reaction function is the fourth pillar, which represents the final outcome of three intertwined drivers – business-cycle dynamics, central bank governance and central bankers’ preferences – and is itself a feedback instrument rule. Then, given the macroeconomic conditions and the infrequent changes of the monetary regime, it is highlighted the role that the central bankers’ preferences has played at various points, describing how, after the founding conservative central banker was born, new members of the Taylor rule family progressively emerged: visionary, prudent, holistic and creative central bankers, respectively with their forward-looking, inertial, augmented, and shadow reaction functions. Finally the literature stresses that so far the true central bankers show a mixed attitude to adopt the flexible instrument rule perspective, particularly when they are confronted with the Odysseus versus Delphi dilemma.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a Tri-Phase Circulating Currency System as an extension of conventional single-phase demurrage currency models. While expiring currencies can promote circulation by weakening the store-of-value function, they often generate psychological resistance, perceived punishment, and institutional distrust due to uniformly imposed expiration mechanisms.To address these limitations, the proposed system decomposes a single currency unit into three phase-states: (i) a basic circulation phase without expiration for everyday stability, (ii) an expiring circulation phase that concentrates the time-cost mechanism, and (iii) a storage phase without expiration for long-term holding and record-keeping. Rather than introducing separate currencies, the system enables cyclical state transitions within one unified currency.A central contribution is an adaptive expiration mechanism applied only to the expiring phase. The expiration period is automatically adjusted based on observed usage within a rolling window—shortening when circulation slows and lengthening when turnover accelerates. This design provides an indirect stabilization channel that aims to moderate inflationary and deflationary pressures through the currency’s time-structure and usage dynamics, without direct manipulation of prices or interest rates.To reduce perceived loss, expired value is institutionally framed as public recirculation and allocated to public-purpose funds or projects. Additional optional transition pathways allow users to convert expiring units via exchanges or combinations with points issued by socially established institutions, while avoiding behavioral evaluation by the currency system itself.The proposal remains conceptual. Future research must formalize the model mathematically, evaluate it through simulation and pilot studies, and examine legal and governance compatibility. By reframing monetary design as a problem of time-structure and circulation architecture, this study offers a structural alternative to traditional stabilization approaches.

detail.abstract: This study examines the evolving geopolitical rivalry between the Republic of Türkiye and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in Somalia and its broader implications for regional dynamics. Utilizing a constructivist theoretical framework, the research analyzes how material power, historical identities, and social norms shape the foreign policy strategies of these two middle powers. Turkey leverages its Ottoman heritage and shared Muslim identity to promote a centralist "One Somalia" policy, focusing on state-building, military training through the TURKSOM base, and energy exploration. In contrast, the UAE pursues a fragmented maritime model, emphasizing stability and economic projection through strategic port investments in Berbera and Bosaso. The study highlights a critical shift in 2026, where diplomatic tensions culminated in Mogadishu's annulment of security pacts with Abu Dhabi and Turkey's deployment of F-16 fighter jets. By integrating qualitative data from bilateral agreements and academic literature, the research contends that the rivalry is not merely a search for regional hegemony but a clash of normative models that significantly influences Somalia's internal political processes and the regional balance of power in the Horn of Africa.

detail.abstract: There is widespread opposition to affirmative action policies. We study whether personal disappointments shape preferences for such policies. Specifically, we test whether individuals' college admissions outcomes, relative to their expectations, influence their attitudes toward affirmative action policies. Using a retrospective survey among recent White and Asian college applicants, we find that disappointed individuals - those who were admitted to fewer schools than anticipated - action policies, and are more willing to donate to an anti-affirmative action organization. They also hold more negative views about the academic qualifications of under-represented minorities. To isolate the causal effect of "bad news" from selection, we conduct a complementary survey experiment with parents of future college applicants. We randomize whether parents receive information about their child's admissions prospects. Providing bad news to overconfident parents causes them to increase opposition to affirmative action and donate to an anti-affirmative action organization. Results suggest that some individuals attribute bad news to external factors, specifically policies that benefit out-groups.

detail.abstract: We build a dynamic quantitative spatial model with mobile households and endogenous fertility to analyze the efficiency of equilibrium fertility choices and city size distribution. We find that the competitive equilibrium is inefficient due to the intergenerational externality. We calibrate our model to German county data and find that excessively large cities have excessively low fertility rates, which yields a 14% welfare loss.

title: Copper Crunch: A Looming Constraint for Energy Policy

detail.title: Copper Crunch: A Looming Constraint for Energy Policy
detail.abstract: Copper, an integral part of the global economy, is utilized extensively across numerous sectors, including construction, telecommunications, and, most notably, the growing renewable energy industry. Recent projections indicate an impending copper supply shortage due to increasing demand driven by global decarbonization and electrification initiatives. As a result, the "copper crunch" presents significant implications for the global economy, energy policy, and geopolitics. Developing new copper mines is a complex, time-consuming task, necessitating extensive exploration, regulatory approval, and a lengthy lead time, often exceeding a decade. Thus, the potential for rapid increases in copper output to meet supply deficits is severely limited. Regulation is a critical factor in this context. Strict environmental standards, labor laws, and protections for indigenous rights can further extend development timelines and inflate costs. Additionally, resource nationalism, where countries aim to retain control of their natural resources, can complicate matters by imposing export restrictions, increasing taxation, or outright nationalization. Copper-exporting countries increasingly aspire to vertical integration, aiming to create value through expansion into downstream activities such as processing and refining. However, this strategy is fraught with challenges, requiring substantial financial investment, skilled labor, advanced technology, and a conducive regulatory environment, which many developing countries find difficult to provide.

title: Backgrounder: The EU's Artificial Intelligence Act

detail.title: Backgrounder: The EU's Artificial Intelligence Act
detail.abstract: The European Union (EU), known for pioneering digital regulation, recently passed the Artificial Intelligence Act (AIA). This comprehensive regulatory scheme represents the first attempt to regulate artificial intelligence. In an effort to understand the AIA's impact on future legislation, this article aims to explore the critical elements of the AIA, the implications for Europe's tech competitiveness, and the geopolitical dimensions surrounding AI regulations, particularly in North America and East Asia.

title: Firm-to-Firm Financial Linkages and Dollar Risk Transmission
affiliations: Bank for International Settlements (BIS) - Monetary and Economic Department, University of Virginia - Darden School of Business and University of California - Davis

detail.title: Firm-to-Firm Financial Linkages and Dollar Risk Transmission
detail.abstract: We study how U.S. dollar fluctuations transmit through domestic supply chains in emerging markets. Large firms borrow in foreign currency and extend trade credit to domestic partners, exposing the supply chain to exchange rate risk. We develop a model where financially constrained suppliers pass through shocks to buyers, while unconstrained firms absorb them. Using quarterly firm-level data from 19 emerging markets, we provide empirical evidence consistent with the model's predictions. We find that even highly exposed firms reduce trade credit only modestly following a depreciation, while accepting large profit losses, suggesting that firm-to-firm credit relationships partially shield downstream firms from financial shocks.

title: Contract Enforcement and Young Firm Capital Structure: A Global Perspective
affiliations: University of New Hampshire and University of California - Davis

detail.title: Contract Enforcement and Young Firm Capital Structure: A Global Perspective
detail.abstract: We develop a framework to measure the severity of financial constraints for young firms across countries. Using ORBIS balance-sheet data for 23 economies, we show that short-term leverage rises while long-term leverage falls early in firms' life cycles, with this pattern persisting longer where contract enforcement is weaker. We build a model of optimal financing under limited enforcement with endogenous debt maturity and blueprint capacity that matches these patterns and enables structural measurement of financial constraints. The framework decomposes the funding gap into within-firm borrowing constraints that ease with repayment history and a scale distortion identifiable through cross-country comparisons.

title: Alliance-Driven Radicalization: A Conceptual Framework for Cross-Institutional Legitimacy Convergence

detail.title: Alliance-Driven Radicalization: A Conceptual Framework for Cross-Institutional Legitimacy Convergence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Zero relationships, just an ordinary Joe.

detail.abstract:
Recent political and social conflicts have unfolded within communicative environments characterized by rapid cross-institutional narrative alignment. Political leaders, media organizations, advocacy networks, and online communities increasingly converge on shared interpretive frames in short time horizons, producing not only information diffusion but also the perception of legitimacy convergence across authority nodes. Existing research has examined ideology, grievance pathways, and online radicalization, yet comparatively little attention has been devoted to how synchrony across institutional actors may shape collective behavior.

This paper proposes a conceptual framework—Alliance-Driven Radicalization—to describe how mutually reinforcing signals across institutions, media, activist networks, and online environments can operate as enabling conditions for mobilization, policy change, and, in rare cases, extreme action. The model identifies a staged mechanism linking institutional signaling, media amplification, activist validation, and networked diffusion to legitimacy convergence and shifts in perceived participation thresholds.

To illustrate the framework, the paper introduces a typology of candidate cases and presents two empirical prototypes: the 2020 United States protest wave and post-2018 bail-reform policy changes in selected jurisdictions. It also develops a negative-case template and boundary-conditions logic to maintain analytical falsifiability and avoid deterministic interpretation.

The framework contributes a synchrony dimension to existing radicalization and contentious-politics models by centering cross-institutional alignment as a distinct mechanism shaping perceived legitimacy and participation boundaries. The paper concludes by outlining directions for future empirical work measuring signaling speed, convergence intensity, counter-signaling effects, and permission diffusion across diverse political contexts.

title: China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan Railway: Better Late than Never

detail.title: China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan Railway: Better Late than Never
detail.abstract: Construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway (CKU) is set to begin in October 2024. First initiated over 27 years ago, this project aims to establish a more direct route connecting China with Central Asia an Europe, enhancing trade and economic integration across these regions. This backgrounder explores the rationale behind the CKU railway and highlights the project's expected geopolitical and economic implications for each of its stakeholders and Eurasian trade in general. The CKU railway project, initially proposed in 1997, has undergone numerous negotiations and revisions. primary objective is to create a direct rail link from China through Kyrgyzstan into Uzbekistan, significantly reducing the transit distance to Europe compared to the traditional Trans-Siberian route.

title: The 3C Model of AI-Driven Accountability Transitions: Chance, Choice, and Change

detail.title: The 3C Model of AI-Driven Accountability Transitions: Chance, Choice, and Change

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the 3C Model of AI-Driven Accountability Transitions, a theoretical framework explaining how AI adoption unfolds through shifts in accountability allocation rather than incremental performance gains. While conventional diffusion models emphasize efficiency improvements, empirical observations across policy, organizational, and technological domains suggest that adoption dynamics are triggered by perceived risk shocks and responsibility renegotiation. The model conceptualizes AI-driven transformation as a three-stage process: Chance (a visible risk trigger destabilizing trust), Choice (reallocation of responsibility between human and algorithmic agents), and Change (institutional adaptation through governance redesign, standardization, and resource rebalancing). Formally, the model proposes that accountability reallocation exerts stronger marginal influence on adoption intensity than performance improvements in high-uncertainty environments. The framework generates testable propositions regarding discontinuous trust collapse, delegation thresholds, and governance rigidity effects. By reframing AI diffusion as an accountability transition problem, the 3C model provides an analytical bridge between AI governance, techno-economic modeling, and institutional change research, offering a structured foundation for empirical and policy-oriented investigations.

title: Trade Models, Trade Elasticities, and the Gains from Trade
affiliations: University of California - Davis and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis

detail.title: Trade Models, Trade Elasticities, and the Gains from Trade
detail.abstract: We consider five models of international trade that belong to the class of models in which the trade elasticity and domestic trade share are sufficient statistics for the welfare cost of autarky. Three are fixed-variety models featuring increasing micro-level margins of adjustment: versions of the Armington model, the Ricardian model, and its variable-markup counterpart. Two are endogenous-variety models featuring monopolistic competition: versions of the Krugman model and the Melitz model. For the three fixed-variety models, we show theoretically that, although they imply the same mapping from the trade elasticity to welfare, they imply different mappings from the trade elasticity to observed order statistics of price gaps of identical goods across countries. This result implies that choosing the parameter that governs the elasticity of trade to match the same order statistics in the data differentially impacts each model's measured welfare cost of autarky. We quantify these differences for all five models.

title: In Gold We Trust: Zimbabwe's Gold-Backed Digital Currency

detail.title: In Gold We Trust: Zimbabwe's Gold-Backed Digital Currency
detail.abstract: In response to economic instability and ongoing currency depreciation, Zimbabwe has recently launched a gold-backed digital currency. This innovative approach uses blockchain technology to issue tokens linked to the value of physical gold. The aim is to provide a reliable and secure value holder in a country suffering from frequent hyperinflation and a significantly depreciated local currency.

title: Geopolitics and Protectionism Inflate Uranium Prices

detail.title: Geopolitics and Protectionism Inflate Uranium Prices
detail.abstract: The global uranium market has experienced significant upheaval in recent years, with prices reaching near-record highs driven by a convergence of renewed demand for nuclear energy, geopolitical disruptions, and protectionist policies from key producing nations. This paper analyzes the supply and demand dynamics reshaping uranium markets within the context of intensifying great power competition and energy security concerns. On the demand side, the paper examines the global nuclear renaissance, including over 60 reactors under construction and 110 planned, the emergence of small modular reactors, and the strategic defense applications sustaining structural demand growth. On the supply side, the analysis traces how the US ban on Russian uranium imports, the Nigerien junta's revocation of French mining permits, Russia's expanding influence in African and Central Asian uranium production, and Kazakhstan's decision to raise extraction taxes are collectively constraining available supply and driving prices upward. The paper further explores how the opacity of uranium pricing, the absence of open market trading, and the use of US government waivers through 2027 complicate sanctions enforcement and price discovery. The analysis identifies an emerging bifurcation in the market, with Western-aligned nations facing higher costs from constrained supply while countries like Turkey, India, and China absorb discounted Russian uranium for domestic use or re-export. The paper concludes that medium-term price trajectories remain upward given persistent supply constraints, accelerating carbon reduction targets, and the scalability potential of next-generation reactor technologies.

title: Sticky Gravity
affiliations: University of Bayreuth - Faculty of Law, Business and Economics, University of Bayreuth and University of Warwick - Department of Economics

detail.title: Sticky Gravity
detail.abstract: International trade flows show strong persistence over time. Standard static gravity models cannot rationalize this persistence and lack a micro-foundation for including lagged trade flows as a determinant of current trade. We develop a structural dynamic gravity framework in which persistence arises from firms' sluggish adjustment of destination-specific prices, analogous to sticky prices in macroeconomics but operating at the bilateral level. The model delivers a gravity equation with lagged trade flows as a structural feature rather than an ad hoc add-on. We propose a novel estimation approach for dynamic gravity models that explicitly accounts for persistence. Empirically, we show that ignoring persistence can lead standard gravity estimates to substantially understate the effects of trade policy changes. As an application, we find that the estimated trade impact of regional trade agreements can increase by 30 percent or more once persistence is taken into account.

title: The Northern Sea Route: Russia's Bet on Arctic Shipping

detail.title: The Northern Sea Route: Russia's Bet on Arctic Shipping
detail.abstract: The Northern Sea Route (NSR) is rapidly emerging as a pivotal trade corridor, viewed as an alternative to the overcrowded Suez Canal and the Malacca Strait. As Arctic ice continues to recede due to explorative activities and climate change, Moscow is actively lobbying for the NSR as a shorter and cost-effective link for Eurasia, piquing interest from China and India. The shift is being watched closely by Washington, which has frequently raised concerns about Russia's growing control and ambitions for influence over Arctic trade, albeit without much actionable change to its own efforts to clip Russia's first-mover advantage in the area. Now, amid the return of US President Donald Trump and mounting geopolitical tensions over the Arctic, the Northern Sea Route is emerging as one of the most controversial, impactful, and increasingly viable trade projects in the 21 century. Historical Context and Potential of the Northern Sea Route The Northern Sea Route illustrates how emerging trade and mining opportunities are driving renewed interest in Arctic geopolitics. Though 2024 trade volumes fell well short of Moscow's expectation, longer-term the route may change the way Russia trades with Asia.

title: US-China Decoupling: A Double-Edged Sword for South Korea

detail.title: US-China Decoupling: A Double-Edged Sword for South Korea
detail.abstract: The intensifying trade dispute between the United States and China, particularly within the semiconductor sector, has added layers of complexity for technology exporters worldwide. A notable player caught in this conflict is South Korea, a country whose economy relies heavily on its semiconductor industry and whose geopolitical ties with the US and China create an intricate balancing act. South Korea maintains a commanding position in the global semiconductor market, with industry leaders Samsung and SK Hynix responsible for the majority of worldwide memory chip production. The notable impact of this industry on the nation's economic health is apparent, as electronics form a substantial portion of South Korean exports, with estimates as high as 30%. Furthermore, the US and China represent South Korea's two largest export markets, making any future export bans or stipulations by either side a costly adjustment for South Korean manufacturers.

title: Critical Minerals: Supply Eases as US, Canada Secure Supply Lines

detail.title: Critical Minerals: Supply Eases as US, Canada Secure Supply Lines
detail.abstract: The United States and Canada have been intensifying their efforts to secure critical mineral supplies in an attempt to counterbalance Russia and China's sweeping control over these crucial resources. The strategic push is aimed at bolstering US and Canadian defense, energy, and technology security amidst growing geopolitical tensions that threaten critical supply lines on multiple fronts.

title: Critical Minerals: Global Graphite Supply & Demand

detail.title: Critical Minerals: Global Graphite Supply & Demand
detail.abstract: The 21st century marks a pivotal transition for energy production and consumption, with fossil fuels gradually yielding to a diversified energy mix that increasingly features renewable sources. Amidst this shift, the role of graphite in powering this pivot is both vital and understated. Although graphite may not readily evoke the recognition associated with commodities such as oil or gold, its strategic relevance makes it a critical resource for clean energy. This report investigates graphite's unique attributes, diverse applications, and the market dynamics affecting its geopolitical and economic significance. Graphite Properties and Applications Graphite, a critical mineral in the global market, is primarily available in natural and synthetic forms. Both forms have distinct characteristics, influencing their demand, pricing, extraction methods, and applications, thus significantly impacting the composition of the global graphite market. Natural graphite is sourced directly from the earth and classified as flake, amorphous, and vein graphite, each possessing varying degrees of purity and suitability for different applications. Flake graphite, for instance, is highly sought after in producing lithium-ion batteries. On the other hand, synthetic graphite is an artificial product created by a more energy-intensive process of heating high-carbon substances like petroleum coke at high temperatures. In addition to higher production costs than natural graphite, the synthetic version possesses higher purity levels and consistency in quality. As a result, synthetic graphite is preferred in end-use applications demanding extreme precision, such as aerospace manufacturing and nuclear energy production.

title: A Middle East BRI? Behind Iraq's $17 Billion "Development Road"

detail.title: A Middle East BRI? Behind Iraq's $17 Billion "Development Road"
detail.abstract: Iraq has unveiled an ambitious $17 billion multimodal transportation project, the "Development Road," designed to connect Europe with the Middle East via a corridor stretching from the Gulf coast to the northern border with Turkey. This paper examines the geopolitical and economic ramifications of the project, which, if realized, would position Iraq as a regional transportation hub and potential competitor to the Suez Canal. The analysis situates the Development Road within the broader landscape of Eurasian connectivity initiatives, drawing comparisons to China's Belt and Road Initiative and the International North-South Transport Corridor while identifying key distinctions, particularly the unresolved question of financing. The paper assesses how the project could catalyze a realignment of regional alliances, with historically rival states such as Iran, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey sharing overlapping interests in the venture, while simultaneously intensifying competition for influence over the emerging hub. The analysis further examines the roles of external powers, including China's strategic interest in developing an alternative to the Suez Canal consistent with BRI objectives, Saudi Arabia's $3 billion investment commitment targeting Iraqi industries, and the European Union's growing demand for diversified energy transit routes amid sanctions on Russian imports. The paper identifies critical challenges to implementation, including skepticism about Iraq's viability as an efficient transit node, the fragility of its political and economic environment, and the difficulty of competing for capital against established Asian connectivity initiatives. The paper concludes that the project's prospects ultimately depend on Iraq's capacity to resolve internal governance challenges and navigate the competing interests of regional and global stakeholders.

title: Sovereign Wealth as Soft Power: Checkbook Diplomacy in the Trump Era

detail.title: Sovereign Wealth as Soft Power: Checkbook Diplomacy in the Trump Era
detail.abstract: In February 2025, the Trump administration signed an executive order directing the development of a United States sovereign wealth fund (SWF), signaling a significant expansion of executive economic power. This paper examines the proposed US fund within the context of a global transformation in sovereign wealth management, arguing that SWFs are no longer passive vehicles for fiscal stabilization or surplus investment but have become active instruments of diplomacy, industrial policy, and geopolitical competition. Drawing on cases from the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Indonesia, China, and Norway, the paper traces how sovereign capital is being deployed to secure supply chains, cultivate elite networks, advance defense priorities, and hedge against de-dollarization. The analysis identifies two critical unresolved questions surrounding the US proposal: capitalization mechanisms, including tariff revenues, federal asset sales, and visa-for-cash programs that would bypass congressional appropriations, and the absence of governance safeguards, oversight structures, or a defined mandate. The paper concludes that a US sovereign wealth fund, even without conventional fiscal surplus justification, would accelerate the politicization of global capital flows and deepen strategic competition over critical sectors and technologies.

title: Progress Share Index (PSh Index, PShI, or PSh)
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Progress Share Index (PSh Index, PShI, or PSh)

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based on the analysis of secondary macroeconomic data and theoretical modeling. It does not involve human participants, patients, or clinical trials, and therefore did not require ethics committee approval.
