The old approach is not effective in reflecting intricate trends across stores and products. In this research, the regression model is random forest, which is applied to estimate the daily sales based on the synthetic data that models 2 years of B2B transaction. The model produced RMSE = 57.50 and MAE = 48.38 which shows the validity in terms of following trends and seasonal variations. The model is effective as demonstrated through visualization of predicted and actual sales against sales made per day. Results show that AI-based forecasting can enhance the decision-making process of operations and maximization of revenues.

title: Technology's Catch-22? A Theory of Zero-Sum Autonomy
affiliations: , Institute of Behavioral Science and Technology, University of St.Gallen and Department of Management and Marketing, University of Melbourne

detail.title: Technology's Catch-22? A Theory of Zero-Sum Autonomy
detail.abstract: Autonomous products-robot vacuums, smart home systems, self-driving vehicles-represent an expanding product class, yet consumer acceptance lags behind technological capability and marketing spending. We introduce the Theory of Zero-Sum Autonomy to explain this gap. The theory's core construct, zero-sum autonomy construal (ZAC), is a relational judgment in which consumers interpret gains in product autonomy as losses of their own autonomy. Consumerautonomous product interaction is susceptible to this construal because autonomy as the product's fundamental functional capacity (independent action) and the consumer's psychological need (self-determination) is shared. The Theory of Zero-Sum Autonomy offers an integrative and relational evaluation of autonomous product interaction that complements our current understanding of autonomous product acceptance. Across five studies (N = 3,067), including representative surveys conducted with industry partners and lab and online experiments, we demonstrate that ZAC is prevalent across consumer segments, consequential for product acceptance, and malleable through marketing communication. Two interventions derived from the theory target its assumptions directly. Reframing autonomy as expandable pie dissolves the finite resource assumption underlying ZAC. Aligning product autonomy with consumer goals restructures the perceived relationship from competitive to cooperative.

title: Using Generative AI and Agentic AI to Unlock Potential of Data-Driven Leadership and Democratize Traditional AI
affiliations: University of Minnesota - Minneapolis and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Using Generative AI and Agentic AI to Unlock Potential of Data-Driven Leadership and Democratize Traditional AI
detail.abstract: Despite an explosion in corporate data generation and the proliferation of business analytics programs, less than 3% of this data is used for decision-making. This paradox reveals a leadership crisis: while data grows exponentially, leaders are failing to leverage it, driven by inertia, ignorance, and a lack of imagination. How do the Three I's inhibit leaders? This paper digs into this question one by one. Based on our industry consulting and research experience, we believe that over the next 2-3 years, traditional AI such as machine learning, predictive analytics, and optimization will continue to generate the majority of business value relative to Generative AI. That being said, it is important to recognize that Generative AI brings complementary opportunities such as accelerating ideation, enhancing personalization, and streamlining knowledge work that can augment existing AI deployments. Organizations that start experimenting responsibly with GenAI today will be better positioned to integrate these capabilities alongside traditional AI, capturing early efficiencies while preparing for larger-scale transformation in the medium to long term. If Generative AI represents the current frontier, agentic AI marks the next one and understanding where it fits in the ‘House of AI’ is an important conceptual task for senior leaders.

title: Financial Market Reactions to the US-Israel Attacks on Iran
affiliations: Westminster International University in Tashkent (WIUT), Abdullah Al Salem University and VALORIZA-Research Center for Endogenous Resource Valorization

detail.title: Financial Market Reactions to the US-Israel Attacks on Iran
detail.abstract: This study investigates the financial market response to the recent US-Israel attack on Iran using an event study and entropy-based framework across key industry sectors and commodities. For event study, we employ both the market model and mean-adjusted model and show significant heterogeneity in cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) across industries. The empirical results show that airlines sector represents large and persistent negative CARs (up to-17.7%), while oil and energy-related commodities show strong positive reactions, with crude oil futures increasing by over 36% in the [0,14] window. In addition, renewable energy and defense sectors display mixed and delayed responses, confirming uncertainty and gradual information diffusion. Overall, negative abnormal returns dominate in the short-to-medium period, indicating an overall adverse market sentiment. Furthermore, robust analysis using approximate entropy reveals a substantial decline in market complexity (-84% to-90%) across all sectors, emphasizing heightened predictability and systemic stress following the major geopolitical event.

detail.abstract: The success and sustainability of an organization, particularly in the dynamic technology sector, are intrinsically linked to the quality of its management. This article examines the impact of effective management practices on the organizational success of Fingertips Plus Technology, a technology startup. Utilizing the Planning, Organizing, Leading, and Controlling (POLC) framework, this case study analyzes how the company's strategic application of management principles fostered a culture of innovation, adaptability, and performance. The research combines a qualitative analysis of the company's strategic trajectory with quantitative data from an employee survey (N=20). Findings indicate that structured planning, clear organizational design, motivational leadership, and robust control mechanisms were pivotal in navigating early-stage challenges and achieving market competitiveness. The study reveals high levels of employee satisfaction regarding role clarity, goal alignment, and workplace culture, which correlates with the company's growth and eventual strategic acquisition. This case demonstrates that a foundational commitment to management principles is a critical determinant of a startup's ability to scale and achieve long-term success.

detail.abstract:
Contemporary economies operate under a growing structural paradox: despite unprecedented advances in information systems, accounting standards, and supervisory capacity, it has become increasingly difficult to distinguish economically legitimate activity from formally compliant yet economically inconsistent transactional flows. This paradox does not arise from regulatory scarcity or informational deficits, but from limitations in how economic validation is conceptually organized within complex institutional systems.

This paper introduces the Systemic Model of Distributed Economic Validation (MSVED) as a systemic-level analytical framework in which economic legitimacy is defined as an emergent property of inter-domain coherence across institutional representations of a given economic transaction. Under the MSVED, validation does not operate as an ex post verification based solely on formal compliance, but as an inter-domain assessment of coherence among accounting, financial, fiscal, and governance domains.

The distinction between strategic equilibrium and the MSVED is not merely methodological, but ontological: while equilibrium defines stability as an emergent property of aligned strategic expectations under given incentives, the MSVED defines legitimacy as an emergent property of inter-domain coherence across institutional representations. From this distinction follows a dual criterion of stability for institutionally dense economies: behavioral stability under incentives and verifiable inter-domain coherence.

This paper contributes to institutional economics by introducing a structural validation framework that complements equilibrium-based reasoning in the analysis of economic legitimacy.

title: Why Systems Can't Fix Themselves: The Missing Redesign Layer

detail.abstract:
“Self-correcting system” is not a single category. It is a bucket label applied to multiple correction layers that are often discussed as if they were one coherent thing. This paper argues that most failing systems do not lack effort, intelligence, data, feedback, governance, or process. They lack a redesign layer. Systems usually do not fail because they cannot react. They fail because they react at the wrong layer.

The paper separates three distinct forms of correction: execution, diagnosis, and redesign. Execution improves performance within an accepted frame. Diagnosis improves control within an accepted frame. Redesign acts upstream of both by changing the frame itself: the primitive, boundary, interface, function allocation, or invariant that defines what the system takes to be work. This produces the paper’s central claim, the Redesign Law: execution improves performance within a frame, diagnosis improves control within a frame, redesign changes the frame itself, and the first two do not reliably produce the third.

The paper then names correction collapse: the condition that arises when execution and diagnostic loops are forced to absorb structural error without any redesign capacity. It shows how this produces denser process, heavier trace, and greater defensibility without proportionate gains in coherence. Three primary proofs are developed across AI task marketplaces, healthcare, and education, with justice as a boundary confirmation, to show that the pattern travels across domains.

The argument is broader than any single sector. These cases are used as clear specimens of a more general structural problem: systems whose own correction machinery is downstream of the frame that needs to change. This paper is Paper 3 of the Diagnostic Lens Trilogy. Companion papers identify interface-legitimacy mismatch and introduce the Four-Function Law of Scalable Institutions.

detail.abstract:
“Institution” is not a category. It is a bucket label applied to structurally different systems, and that surface naming hides a recurring structural failure pattern. This paper argues that institutions do not fail under scale because they are large, busy, or imperfectly managed. They fail when irreducible functions remain fused at the point of consequence.

The paper breaks institutional work into four irreducible functions: sensing, interpretation, authority, and memory. If an institution persists through time, receives inputs from reality, makes decisions, and claims continuity, these functions exist somewhere in its structure. They cannot be eliminated. They can only be distributed across structures, encoded into protocol, or collapsed into humans. Failure appears when multiple functions remain fused in the same human node under ambiguity and consequence, without effective offloading, contestability, or continuity support. This paper names that condition collapse.

The paper distinguishes operational memory from audit memory, introduces the Function Placement Test as a diagnostic instrument, and names a predictable cascade that follows unresolved function fusion: personalisation of responsibility, documentation inflation, process sprawl, exception overload, informal substitution, and legibility inversion. It then develops two primary proofs, healthcare and education, and boundary confirmations from law and end-of-life care to show that the pattern travels across domains.

The argument is broader than any single institution. Healthcare, education, and law are used as clear specimens of a more general structural problem: systems whose burdens are misclassified as workload, shortage, bureaucracy, or burnout when the deeper issue is bad function allocation. This paper is Paper 2 of the Diagnostic Lens Trilogy. Companion papers identify interface-legitimacy mismatch and explain why execution and diagnosis cannot reliably generate redesign from within the same correction loops.

detail.abstract: Conventional market entry and diffusion frameworks typically assume that demand emerges progressively as awareness increases and access expands. However, empirical observation across complex multi-stakeholder markets reveals persistent discontinuities between awareness, trial, and sustained adoption. Products frequently achieve visibility yet fail to generate demand, or achieve trial without scalable market access. This paper introduces the Demand Barrier Market Access Map (D-B MAM), a structural model that explains demand formation and market access as a network-based threshold process governed by cumulative resistance across multiple decision-making stakeholders. Adoption occurs only when cumulative resistance falls below the Demand Formation Threshold at each node and propagates sequentially through the stakeholder network. Post-activation sustainability is governed by operational and institutional constraints. The framework provides a mechanistic explanation of discontinuous adoption, conversion failure, and systemic collapse. It offers a structural diagnostic model for analyzing market access, adoption failure, and scaling constraints across both B2B and B2C environments.

title: Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Document Standardization in Financial Services: A Systematic Literature Review

detail.title: Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Document Standardization in Financial Services: A Systematic Literature Review
detail.abstract: In contemporary business environments, financial organizations face significant challenges in managing heterogeneous document formats, leading to inefficiencies, human errors, and increased operational costs. This systematic literature review examines the impact of generative artificial intelligence (AI) on document standardization, analysis, and processing within financial services. Through comprehensive analysis of recent literature (2022-2026) and comparative case studies from industry implementations, this work identifies how multimodal large language models transform document management workflows. The review synthesizes findings from academic publications and industry reports, focusing on two major case studies: a multinational professional services firm's AI implementation and analyses from international economic organizations. Results demonstrate that generative AI systems achieve efficiency improvements of 70-80 percent in document processing tasks, while significantly reducing manual errors and enabling automated extraction from diverse document formats. This work contributes a structured framework for understanding AI-driven document standardization and provides evidence-based insights for financial institutions considering AI adoption.

detail.title: Visions of Sovereign AI
detail.abstract: This report provides a comprehensive, asset-level analysis of AI sovereignty across twelve countries and blocs: the United States, China, South Korea, Japan, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, the European Union, Singapore, Israel, Australia, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. We introduce an autonomy–resilience framework that evaluates each state's control over AI capabilities and its ability to sustain them amid external shocks, and analyzes positioning across six supply chain segments: energy, compute, chips, data, models, and critical minerals. Our comparative assessment identifies a sovereignty spectrum ranging from fully sovereign through partially sovereign and dependent states, and finds that full-stack AI sovereignty is exceptionally rare. For most nations, the realistic strategic path runs through cultivating indispensability within an allied supply chain rather than pursuing autarky. The report concludes with strategic recommendations for U.S. policymakers, including the creation of certified full-stack integrators for AI exports, financing facilities and investment vehicles, and urgent domestic actions to close gaps in energy infrastructure, high-bandwidth memory production, and critical minerals processing.

detail.abstract:
“AI task platform” is not a category. It is a bucket label applied to several structurally different systems, and that naming collision hides a recurring design error. Many platforms that appear to recruit for expertise operate instead as reliability pipelines: systems engineered to suppress variance through qualification gates, unitised work, and continuous quality control. The result is an expertise illusion. Contributors enter expecting their judgment to be valued, while the system primarily consumes instruction adherence under constraint.

This paper argues that many AI task marketplaces recruit through the legitimacy grammar of expert sourcing while optimising in execution for constrained, repeatable judgment. Recruitment signals credibility, skill, and specialist access. Execution optimises for consistency, compliance, and measurable quality control across repeated units of work. The mismatch is not incidental. It is structural.

To make that mismatch portable, the paper introduces the Transfer Test: compare what a system optimises for in execution with what it signals in recruitment or interface. If the answers diverge, the same class of mismatch is present. The paper then shows how this error produces systematic misrecognition. Reliable executors are the true operating need. Credentialed specialists are often filtered in but only partially consumed. Upstream reframing capability—the capacity to question malformed task boundaries, categories, and invariants—has no native recognition channel inside the marketplace.

The argument is broader than AI labour markets. These platforms are a clean specimen of a more general pattern: systems that recruit for one kind of work while consuming another, and that compensate for the mismatch with process rather than redesign. This paper is Paper 1 of the Diagnostic Lens Trilogy. Companion papers introduce the Four-Function Law of Scalable Institutions and explain why execution and diagnosis cannot reliably generate redesign from within the same correction loops.

detail.abstract:
Firms operating in mature markets face a persistent paradox: they continue to improve, yet struggle to remain distinguishable. Conventional explanations attribute this condition to failures of marketing execution. This paper advances an alternative hypothesis: the problem is structural rather than operational.

The paper introduces three core concepts—structural saturation, category as institution, and meaning scarcity—to explain why differentiation systematically erodes as markets mature. Structural saturation refers to the condition in which competitive positions within a category become fully occupied and replicable, rendering incremental improvement strategically ineffective. Building on institutional theory, categories are reconceptualized as systems of interpretation that govern how value is defined and evaluated, shaping both firm behavior and the limits of differentiation. Under these conditions, convergence emerges not as a failure of strategy, but as a rational response to institutional constraints.
As functional attributes diffuse and become standardized, their capacity to produce distinction declines. Meaning, by contrast, cannot be industrialized—and therefore cannot be replicated or diffused at the same rate—emerging as the only structurally scarce dimension of competition. The paper thus reframes the shift from functional to symbolic competition as a structural outcome rather than a change in consumer preferences.

By integrating institutional theory with strategic management and branding research, the paper provides a diagnostic framework for understanding differentiation failure in mature markets. The central implication is that firms are not failing to compete effectively, but may be competing at a level that no longer determines their ability to stand out.

title: Name, Image, Likeness And The Great American Pastime

detail.title: Name, Image, Likeness And The Great American Pastime
detail.abstract: The ability of high-profile athletes to commercialize name, image, and likeness (NIL) rights is at the center of many current controversies about the future of college sports in the United States. This Article describes how what we call NIL protection-largely based on publicity rights doctrines developed in the mid-20th century-is historically recent, conceptually unstable, and insufficiently scrutinized, even though it now underwrites major entertainment markets in sports. Just as baseball is a sport particularly identified with the United States, there is also a peculiarly American approach to the protection of persona. Using baseball as the central case study, the Article traces how commercialization around bats, branding, baseball cards, broadcasting, and player endorsements generated recurring disputes that helped push U.S. law from privacy-based protection toward an alienable, property-like right of publicity, crystallized in the case of Haelan Labs v. Topps. The Article then contrasts this American approach to publicity rights with the development of the English law in order to demonstrate that broad, transferable NIL rights are not an inevitable common-law development. Finally, the Article argues that the expansive regime of state-by-state publicity rights offers doctrinally incoherent protection at a significant social cost. It sketches an alternative: a more limited, non-alienable privacy-based protection to protect dignitary rights, supplemented by a passing off tort to protect commercial goodwill interests in personal identity.

title: Legal Implications of Artificial Intelligence: A Comparative Analysis of Global Regulatory Frameworks and Emerging Challenges

detail.title: Legal Implications of Artificial Intelligence: A Comparative Analysis of Global Regulatory Frameworks and Emerging Challenges
detail.abstract: The accelerated development of artificial intelligence has outpaced the capacity of traditional legal frameworks to address its implications, generating unprecedented challenges in liability attribution, data protection, intellectual property rights, and algorithmic fairness. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the main regulatory frameworks that have emerged internationally to govern AI development and deployment. We examine the European Union's horizontal, risk-based approach embodied in the AI Act and its interplay with the GDPR, contrasting it with the United States' sectoral, voluntary framework articulated through Executive Order 14110 and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. We also analyze international standardization initiatives led by UNESCO, OECD, and ISO/IEC. Our findings reveal fundamental tensions between innovation and regulation, highlighting critical legal gaps in civil and criminal liability attribution, intellectual property rights for AIgenerated content, algorithmic bias mitigation, and transparency obligations. We conclude that the technical complexity of AI systems, diversity of national ethical frameworks, and conflicting economic interests hinder global regulatory harmonization, requiring flexible and updatable regulatory approaches that balance citizen protection with technological advancement.

title: FDI in Ethiopia: Is "Abiymania" Enough?

detail.abstract: Following his ascension to the position of prime minister, Abiy Ahmed's commitment to enact a series of lofty reforms designed to modernize Ethiopia's economy has attracted a considerable amount of foreign direct investment into the country. Recent figures suggest that Ethiopia alone accounts for over 33% of all FDI within East Africa. With recorded FDI inflows reaching $3.3 billion USD in 2018, the Ethiopian Investment Commission, a governmental body, has projected an increase of up to $5.1 billion USD in attracted investment. detail.abstract: This paper presents the implementation of IT Service Management (ITSM) methodologies in the context of incident management services at a Costa Rican technology services company. The research focuses on identifying operational deficiencies affecting the handling of requests and incidents on a technological platform used by public hospitals in Costa Rica. Through the ITIL v4 reference framework, processes, roles, tools, and communication channels are evaluated, prioritizing continuous service improvement through structured, end-user-oriented practices. Analysis of 1,150 tickets over six months revealed that 52.3% experience more than two transfers, with critical incidents reaching 76.1%. Results show significant deficiencies in process documentation (2.3/5), escalation levels (2.0/5), and inter-organizational communication (2.5/5). The improvement proposal includes help desk unification, escalation flow redesign, and performance indicator implementation, targeting an average resolution time reduction to 4 hours and 90% SLA compliance.

title: Implementation of the OCTAVE Methodology: A Comprehensive Guide for Information Technology Risk Management in Industrial Environments

detail.title: Implementation of the OCTAVE Methodology: A Comprehensive Guide for Information Technology Risk Management in Industrial Environments
detail.abstract: This paper presents the OCTAVE (Operationally Critical Threat, Asset, and Vulnerability Evaluation) methodology and provides a comprehensive implementation guide for the industry. Developed by the Software Engineering Institute (SEI) at Carnegie Mellon University, OCTAVE is a risk assessment framework focused on the identification, analysis, and mitigation of risks, prioritizing critical information assets and their vulnerabilities. The objective of this study is to apply OCTAVE to improve the protection of information assets, strengthen organizational resilience, and ensure compliance with security regulations. The paper is structured around three main phases: identification of critical assets, analysis of threats and vulnerabilities, and development of risk mitigation strategies. Implementation of OCTAVE enables effective identification and management of information security risks. The recommendations provided contribute to a stronger security posture, ensuring operational continuity for organizations facing an increasingly challenging environment of risks and threats. This study establishes a foundation for future risk management efforts, promoting continuous improvement of security practices. A detailed case study from the manufacturing sector demonstrates the practical application and effectiveness of OCTAVE in industrial control systems environments.

title: CYBERSECURITY POSTURE MISREPRESENTATION AND FALSE CLAIMS ACT LIABILITY: SPRS SCORE ACCURACY AND THE ESCOBAR MATERIALITY PROBLEM

detail.title: CYBERSECURITY POSTURE MISREPRESENTATION AND FALSE CLAIMS ACT LIABILITY: SPRS SCORE ACCURACY AND THE ESCOBAR MATERIALITY PROBLEM
detail.abstract:
The Department of Justice's Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative has produced fifteen False Claims Act settlements since October 2021 - nine in fiscal year 2025 alone, recovering more than $52 million - centered on the accuracy of cybersecurity compliance representations submitted through the Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement's Supplier Performance Risk System. Every enforcement matter to date has resolved through settlement without a merits ruling, leaving the enforcement record uniformly settlement-based and the underlying doctrine unresolved.

This working paper advances a focused argument: that SPRS score submissions made pursuant to DFARS 252.204-7019, when materially inaccurate and maintained with knowledge of that inaccuracy, may satisfy the elements of FCA implied false certification liability under Universal Health Services, Inc. v. United States ex rel. Escobar, 579 U.S. 176 (2016). The analysis locates materiality as the dispositive doctrinal question and examines four contested elements: the government-knowledge defense, the continued-payment doctrine, the express-versus-implied conditions distinction, and the systemic-versus-minor compliance gap framework.

The paper introduces SPRS-Based Compliance Representation Liability as an independently citable analytical sub-theory synthesizing the enforcement record and Escobar doctrine, identifies five conditions for cognizable FCA exposure, and provides the first systematic academic synthesis of an enforcement area that has generated more than $100 million in recoveries without a single adjudicated precedent. The framework stands as the analytical baseline until a court rules on the merits.

title: Digital Transformation in Solidarity Organizations: Application of DevOps, Lean, and Scrum Frameworks for IT Management

detail.title: Digital Transformation in Solidarity Organizations: Application of DevOps, Lean, and Scrum Frameworks for IT Management
detail.abstract: This study addresses IT management challenges faced by a Costa Rican solidarity association experiencing rapid growth, through the application of DevOps, Lean, and Scrum frameworks. The organization operates with a fragmented technological model, 80% manual processes, and complete outsourcing of IT functions, resulting in slow value delivery to its 800+ members. Using Value Stream Mapping, we identified critical inefficiencies with process efficiency of only 2.5% in credit management workflows. We propose six integrated improvement initiatives: establishing an internal agile IT team, automating critical processes, implementing basic CI/CD pipelines, creating business intelligence dashboards, institutionalizing continuous improvement retrospectives, and adopting agile management tools. The expected outcomes include reducing cycle times from 7-10 days to less than 24 hours for member onboarding, increasing deployment frequency from quarterly to monthly, and achieving process efficiency improvements exceeding 60%. This research demonstrates that DevOps-Lean-Scrum integration is highly applicable to small organizations with limited IT maturity, providing a pragmatic roadmap for incremental digital transformation in the solidarity sector.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the effectiveness of the CFIUS real estate review regime-the federal government's primary mechanism for screening foreign agricultural land acquisitions near military installations-by measuring what fraction of documented Chinese-linked agricultural holdings actually fall within CFIUS jurisdiction. Using a novel geocoded database of all 230 installations listed in CFIUS Appendix A across four successive regulatory regimes (2018-2024), matched against 171 Chinese-linked agricultural holdings from USDA AFIDA data across 119 counties, the analysis finds that even under the most expansive current rules (effective December 2024), 50.4 percent of counties holding 33.1 percent of acreage remain outside CFIUS jurisdiction. The 1-mile proximity threshold (Part 1) covers zero agricultural holdings; all coverage derives from the 100-mile extended range (Part 2). The 2024 expansionwhich added 59 installations-captured only 6 additional counties, while a site replacement in Iowa created a coverage regression that dropped 4 Missouri counties (35,867 acres) outside the perimeter. A previously unrecognized structural gap emerges from the Part 1/Part 2 classification: 30 counties are within 100 miles of a Part 1 installation but outside jurisdiction because Part 1 carries only a 1-mile threshold; reclassifying all Part 1 sites to Part 2 would increase coverage from 49.6 to 74.8 percent without adding a single new installation. Multiplying the jurisdictional gap by the 92.7 percent beneficial ownership visibility gap documented in the companion paper yields an effective federal detection probability of approximately 3.6 percent. A multi-threshold boundary discontinuity analysis at 25, 50, 75, 100, and 125 miles finds no statistically significant density discontinuities, though directional 1 asymmetry at the 100-mile threshold is suggestive. A difference-indifferences analysis of 21 state-level restrictions cannot isolate treatment effects from the concurrent 54 percent decline in Chinese-attributed holdings driven by USDA data reclassification. The Sun Guangxin caseapproximately 130,000 acres acquired near Laughlin Air Force Base through a Texas limited partnership while Texas granted aliens equal property rights, CFIUS had no jurisdiction, and the ownership structure was invisible to federal analysis-illustrates all three dimensions of the compound gap in a single documented acquisition.

detail.title: Agentic Supply Chain Control Towers: A Framework for Autonomous and Resilient Operations
detail.abstract: Contemporary supply chains operate in a disruption-prone environment where traditional systems, including Supply Chain Control Towers (SCCTs), struggle to ensure resilience. These systems are hindered by two core challenges: 1) data fragmentation and quality issues, which prevent a unified view, and 2) a critical analysis-to-action gap, which delays response by relying on manual intervention. This paper addresses these dual challenges by proposing the "Agentic Supply Chain Control Tower" framework. Using a design science research methodology, this framework features a Digital Twin Tier to mitigate fragmentation and a Cognition Tier containing a workforce of autonomous AI agents to bridge the action gap. The framework's capabilities are validated through a proof-of-concept, demonstrating potential for unified sensing, advanced reasoning, and governed autonomous action. The findings present a new approach for supply chain management based on autonomous orchestration, offering a pathway to more resilient operations.

detail.abstract: Despite active federal legislation targeting foreign agricultural land purchases near U.S. military installations, no peer-reviewed study has applied formal spatial hypothesis testing to the core empirical question: does the observed proximity pattern exceed random chance, and is it specific to adversarial-nation investors? This paper addresses both questions using USDA Agricultural Foreign Investment Disclosure Act (AFIDA) detailed holdings data for 2020 through 2024 — the federal government's primary record of foreign agricultural land ownership. I apply Monte Carlo permutation testing to holdings attributed to 11 investor countries, geocoded to county centroids and tested against 71 CONUS military installations and critical infrastructure sites.  The central finding is comparative. All foreign agricultural holdings exhibit moderately elevated proximity to installations (1.7–2.0× enrichment for allied nations including Canada, UK, Netherlands, Germany, and Italy), reflecting the co-location of military sites and farmland in rural areas. However, Chinese-attributed holdings cluster at 3.4× enrichment at 50 miles (p < 0.001) — nearly twice the allied-nation baseline of 1.8×. Saudi Arabian holdings also show elevated clustering (2.6×, p = 0.005). This differential clustering — significant for adversarial-nation investors but not explained by agricultural geography alone — is the paper's primary contribution. Restricting to nuclear-capable installations (ICBM fields, bomber bases, submarine bases, DOE weapons complex), Chinese holdings show 12.7× enrichment. Results survive four robustness checks. Panel analysis (2022–2024) reveals declining mean distances as total acreage decreases, suggesting proximate holdings persist while distant ones are divested. Ownership is concentrated (HHI = 1,880), with five entities controlling 88% of Chinese-attributed acreage.  These findings provide the first formal empirical foundation — derived from federal primary-source data with multi-country comparative benchmarking — for the policy assumption underlying the PASS Act, CFIUS real estate jurisdiction expansion, and 26 state-level foreign land ownership restrictions. All data are publicly available from the USDA and NOAA. All code is open-source.

English Abstract: The article calls for rethinking the legal tools available to the state in addressing public corruption. Instead of relying almost exclusively on criminal law, it highlights the underexplored potential of fiduciary law as an independent enforcement mechanism. It argues that overreliance on criminal enforcement creates two risks: first, it may foster the perception that conduct is permissible so long as it is not criminal; and second, it may lead to the use of criminal law even where it is ill-suited, whether due to evidentiary challenges or because the conduct does not meet the criminal threshold, out of concern that the public official will otherwise escape liability for corrupt conduct. As an alternative, the article proposes expanding the use of civil actions based on breach of fiduciary duty, even in the absence of a criminal conviction. It presents the doctrinal foundations for classifying public officials as fiduciaries, explores the normative justifications for this approach, and addresses institutional constraints that may hinder its implementation.

detail.abstract: Online food delivery services have become an integral part of consumers' daily lives due to increased smartphone usage and changing lifestyles. In such a competitive environment, understanding customer satisfaction is essential for service providers. This study examines the influence of service quality dimensions and value-oriented factors on customer satisfaction in online food delivery services. Primary data were collected from 260 users of online food delivery applications through a structured questionnaire based on a five-point Likert scale. The data were analysed using statistical tools such as correlation analysis, multiple regression analysis, and one-way ANOVA with the help of SPSS software. The results indicate that tangibility, empathy, and price-saving orientation significantly influence customer satisfaction, while other service quality dimensions show a limited impact. The study also finds that income level creates a significant difference in satisfaction, whereas age, frequency of usage, and platform preference do not. The findings provide useful insights for online food delivery companies to improve customer satisfaction through better service design and pricing strategies.

detail.title: The Contribution of Lord Cornwallis To Make the Indian Judicial System More Organize and Fairer
detail.abstract: This article explains the contribution of Lord Cornwallis in making the Indian judicial system more organized and fair. Before his reforms, the system was confusing and corrupt. The same officers handled both revenue and judicial work, which caused misuse of power and injustice. Cornwallis introduced reforms in 1787, 1790, and 1793. He reorganized civil and criminal courts, increased judges' salaries to reduce corruption, and most importantly separated the judiciary from the executive through the Cornwallis Code of 1793. He also created proper courts at district and provincial levels and made laws more clear and systematic. Although Indians were mostly excluded from higher posts, his reforms laid the foundation of a modern, rule-based judicial system in India.

title: Heavy-Duty Electric Vehicle Charging Scheduling at Community Charging Hubs
affiliations: , Independent and WHU - Otto Beisheim School of Management

detail.title: Heavy-Duty Electric Vehicle Charging Scheduling at Community Charging Hubs
detail.abstract:
The deployment of heavy-duty battery-electric trucks and buses is accelerating. Sufficient charging infrastructure is a critical enabler of this growth, particularly at depots and warehouses, where most charging is expected to occur. However, such infrastructure requires substantial investment and entails long lead times. We therefore introduce Community Charging Hubs, a novel concept for centrally coordinated charging, shared among firms located within the same logistics park. 
We formulate a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) to maximize hub operator profit when scheduling vehicles on a limited, shared set of chargers, and we propose a novel Assign-and-Optimize matheuristic to solve large-scale instances efficiently. Using a logistics park in Switzerland with up to 120 battery-electric trucks and buses, we show charging price reductions of up to 51% and peak load reductions up to 80% for participating firms. Benefits are particularly pronounced in the early electrification phase, for small to mid-scale fleets. We incorporate hourly on-site photovoltaic (PV) generation and electricity spot prices and show that an appropriately sized PV system contributes materially to these reductions. By contrast, under typical operations, hourly spot prices yield only marginal additional gains and only when excess grid capacity is available. These findings also hold when charger reservations are considered.

title: The Harm Blindness Framework: A Practical Application Methodology for Stakeholder Harm Prevention in Technology Development
affiliations: Real Safety AI Foundation

detail.title: The Harm Blindness Framework: A Practical Application Methodology for Stakeholder Harm Prevention in Technology Development

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Technology development consistently produces preventable harm to stakeholders who were identifiable at the time of key decisions. This paper introduces the Harm Blindness Framework, a checkpoint-based methodology designed to surface stakeholder impacts during development rather than after deployment. The framework operationalizes consultation of historical precedent through structured analysis at four decision points: ideation, design, testing, and launch. Validation against 161 historical cases spanning approximately 5,000 years reveals that 95.7% of analyzed harms had documented precedent available at the time decisions were made. The remaining 4.3% represent genuinely first-of-kind situations. A parallel analysis of 151 corporate disasters from 1970-2025 demonstrates that prevention costs typically range from 1-10% of eventual disaster costs, yielding return-on-investment ratios of 1,000-10,000x for harm prevention. The framework is designed to function regardless of whether implementing organizations are motivated by ethical concerns or risk management objectives. The same analytical methodology surfaces the same stakeholder impacts; only the framing differs. This motivation-agnostic design addresses a significant limitation of existing ethical frameworks, which typically require ethical commitment as a precondition for adoption. This paper presents the theoretical foundation, methodology, validation evidence, and limitations of the framework. Supporting materials including implementation guides, checkpoint templates, and complete validation studies are available separately.

title: Opt-in or Opt-out? The Power of Defaults in Pension Enrollment Choices
affiliations: ZEW – Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research, Max Planck Society for the Advancement of the Sciences - Munich Center for the Economics of Aging (MEA), University of Oslo and Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU)

detail.title: Opt-in or Opt-out? The Power of Defaults in Pension Enrollment Choices
detail.abstract: Default settings strongly increase pension enrollment, especially when savings incentives are high and choices are complex. We show that the effect is weaker when incentives are low, options are simple, and opting out is easy. We study the nationwide introduction of auto-enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pay-as-you-go pension system. We find that automatic enrollment raises participation by 23 percentage points, though most individuals actively opt out. Linking administrative and survey data shows that the default effect is stronger when enrollment incentives are higher and among individuals who lack knowledge of their enrollment status.
